tamil:
கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார் கேண்மை அடுங்காலை
உள்ளினும் உள்ளஞ் சுடும்.
transliteration:
Kedungaalaik kaividuvaar kenmai adungaalai
ullinum ullanj chudum.
current_meaning: Friends who left you when you were in trouble will burn your heart, even if you only think of them at the hour of your death.
elementary: Have you ever been left alone by a friend when you really needed help? That hurt can stay with you for a very long time, even when you are grown up. Valluvar says this hurt is so strong it can burn even at the very end of life.
university: Kedungaalai (கெடுங்காலை) is ‘at the time when one is being ruined’, and adungaalai (அடுங்காலை) is ‘at the time when one is being slain’, the hour of death; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as the time when Yama comes to kill, and Kalaignar reads it as the moment one is being put to death. Ullinum (உள்ளினும், ‘even if one recalls’) and ullam sudum (உள்ளம் சுடும், ‘the heart burns’) make a play on ul- (‘think’) and ullam (‘mind’). The force of the couplet is psychological: the wound of desertion outlasts every other pain, so one should never form such a friendship in the first place, which ties it back to the chapter’s theme of investigation. The sandhi-joined text reads கேண்மை யடுங்காலை யுள்ளினு முள்ளஞ் சுடும், the same words.

tamil:
மருவுக மாசற்றார் கேண்மைஒன் றீத்தும்
ஒருவுக ஒப்பிலார் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Maruvuka maasatraar kenmaion reeththum
oruvuka oppilaar natpu.
current_meaning: Stay close to good people who have no faults. Leave the friendship of the wrong people, even if you have to give something up to do it.
elementary: Think of friends like food. Keep eating the fresh fruit. If something in your lunchbox has gone bad, throw it away, even if you paid for it. Keep good friends close, and let the bad ones go even if that costs you something.
university: The closing couplet balances two imperatives in parallel: maruvuka (மருவுக, ‘cling to, embrace’) and oruvuka (ஒருவுக, ‘leave, shun’). Maasatraar (மாசற்றார்) are ‘those without stain’, while oppilaar (ஒப்பிலார்) is ambiguous: Parimelazhagar takes it as those who do not accord with the world’s good ways, Solomon Pappaiah follows with ‘those who do not fit with the world’, and Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘those who lack matching virtue’. Onru eeththum (ஒன்று ஈத்தும், ‘even by giving something’) mirrors koduththum in kural 794: just as a good friend is worth buying, a bad one is worth paying to be rid of. The ytamizh and thirukkural.net texts read ஈத்தும், while the sandhi-joined edition divides the line as கேண்மையொன் றீத்து மொருவுக, which reads the same once the sandhi is undone.

tamil:
பழைமை எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதும்
கிழமையைக் கீழ்ந்திடா நட்பு.
transliteration:
Pazhaimai enappaduvadhu yaadhenin yaadhum
kizhamaiyaik keezhndhidaa natpu.
current_meaning: What is an old friendship? It is one where you never get upset, in any way, when an old friend acts freely with you because you are close.
elementary: A brand-new classmate has to knock before borrowing your pencil. Your oldest friend just picks it up, and you don’t mind at all. That not-minding is what a really old friendship looks like.
university: The chapter opens with a definition. Pazhaimai (பழைமை, ‘oldness’) is the friendship that has grown old, and kizhamai (கிழமை) is the ‘right’ or ‘claim’ (urimai, உரிமை) that such long intimacy creates; keezhndhidaa (கீழ்ந்திடா) means ‘does not cut down, belittle or set aside’. Read with yaadhum (‘in anything at all’), the couplet says that true old friendship never treats the friend’s presumptions as offences. Parimelazhagar places the chapter directly after Natpaaraaydhal (testing a friend before befriending) and the commentarial tradition reads it as the next stage: once a friend has been tested and kept, the bond should bear the freedoms that time brings. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss the couplet as accepting what the old friend does by right of intimacy, while Puliyur Kesigan reads it more broadly as a friendship that lets nothing damage the established bond. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நட்பிற் குறுப்புக் கெழுதகைமை மற்றதற்கு
உப்பாதல் சான்றோர் கடன்.
transliteration:
Natpir kuruppuk kezhudhakaimai matradharku
uppaadhal saandror kadan.
current_meaning: The freedoms friends take with each other are part of friendship. Good people should welcome those freedoms and enjoy them.
elementary: Salt makes food taste right. In a friendship, the little freedoms friends take, like finishing your sentences or grabbing a fry off your plate, are the salt. A good person does not complain about the salt; they enjoy the meal.
university: Uruppu (உறுப்பு, ‘limb, constituent part’) makes kezhudhakaimai (கெழுதகைமை, ‘the quality of intimate right’) a structural part of friendship, not an extra. The second line turns on uppu (உப்பு, ‘salt’), which the commentators read figuratively as relish or sweetness: the wise should be the salt to that intimacy, accepting it and taking pleasure in it. Mu. Varadarasanar reads uppaadhal as ‘agreeing to’ the friend’s act of right, Solomon Pappaiah as ‘rejoicing at it’, and Puliyur Kesigan as ‘acting as the very model of that intimacy’. G. U. Pope’s ‘to be its savour sweet is duty of the wise’ keeps the image of salt. Saandror (சான்றோர்) are the cultivated people whose kadan (கடன், ‘duty, obligation’) this is. Both base sources give the same text.

tamil:
பழகிய நட்பெவன் செய்யுங் கெழுதகைமை
செய்தாங்கு அமையாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Pazhakiya natpevan seyyung kezhudhakaimai
seydhaangu amaiyaak kadai.
current_meaning: What good is a friendship of many years if you will not accept what your close friend does, as if you had done it yourself?
elementary: Imagine your best friend signs both your names on a birthday card for your teacher without asking. If you get cross, what was all that friendship for? A real friend says, ‘Good idea, that’s what I would have done.’
university: The couplet is a rhetorical question: evan seyyum (எவன் செய்யும், ‘what will it do?’) asks what use a long-practised friendship (pazhakiya natpu) has if one does not seydhaangu amaidhal (செய்தாங்கு அமைதல்), ‘acquiesce as though one had done it oneself’, in what the friend did by kezhudhakaimai (intimate right). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take this as owning the friend’s act; Solomon Pappaiah adds that this holds even when one does not personally agree with it. Puliyur Kesigan reads the line from the other side: if the same intimacy is not present in the friend too, the long acquaintance is useless. That reading shows the couplet can be taken as a statement about reciprocity. The text is the same in both base sources (with the sandhi form seyyung).

tamil:
விழைதகையான் வேண்டி இருப்பர் கெழுதகையாற்
கேளாது நட்டார் செயின்.
transliteration:
Vizhaidhakaiyaan vendi iruppar kezhudhakaiyaar
kelaadhu nattaar seyin.
current_meaning: When close friends do something for you without asking, wise people are happy about it, because it came from someone they love.
elementary: Your friend sees your bike tyre is flat and pumps it up while you are at lunch, without asking. You don’t say, ‘Who gave you permission?’ You say, ‘Thanks!’ That is how old friends treat each other.
university: The key phrase is kelaadhu (கேளாது, ‘without asking’): the friend acts for us kezhudhakaiyaal, ‘by the right of intimacy’. The wise respond vizhaidhakaiyaan (விழைதகையான், ‘because of its desirability’), and vendi iruppar, ‘remain as those who wanted it’. Mu. Varadarasanar emphasises honouring the right itself, while Solomon Pappaiah says the wise accept the act even when they already knew of it, because it was done willingly by a friend. Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesigan make the same point more plainly: a good friend accepts what was done unasked. The couplet assumes a household culture in which a close friend may lawfully use or dispose of what is ours. Both base texts agree.

tamil:
பேதைமை ஒன்றோ பெருங்கிழமை என்றுணர்க
நோதக்க நட்டார் செயின்.
transliteration:
Pedhaimai ondro perungizhamai endrunarka
nodhakka nattaar seyin.
current_meaning: If a friend does something that hurts you, think that it came either from not knowing better or from being so close that they felt free to do it.
elementary: If your best friend borrows your favourite book and spills juice on it, think: ‘Maybe they didn’t know it mattered so much, or maybe they just felt at home with my things.’ Don’t decide straight away that they meant to hurt you.
university: Pedhaimai (பேதைமை, ‘ignorance, folly’) and perungizhamai (பெருங்கிழமை, ‘great intimacy, strong right of friendship’) are the two charitable explanations the couplet offers for an act that is nodhakka (நோதக்க, ‘fit to cause pain’). The particle ondro (ஒன்றோ) divides the commentators. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as ‘either … or’: ignorance or intimacy. Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘not ignorance only, but also great intimacy’. Puliyur Kesigan reads it as rejecting ignorance altogether: think of it as intimacy, not ignorance. The pairing is close to Arjuna’s pramādāt praṇayena vā (‘through carelessness or through affection’) in Bhagavad Gita 11.41, a parallel worth noting even though no direct influence can be shown. The text is the same in both base sources.

tamil:
எல்லைக்கண் நின்றார் துறவார் தொலைவிடத்தும்
தொல்லைக்கண் நின்றார் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Ellaikkan nindraar thuravaar tholaividaththum
thollaikkan nindraar thodarpu.
current_meaning: People who know what true friendship is will not leave old friends, even when that friendship causes them loss.
elementary: Suppose your oldest friend accidentally makes your team lose the big game. A true friend doesn’t say, ‘We’re done.’ They say, ‘We’ve been friends forever, and one bad game won’t change that.’
university: The couplet balances ellai (எல்லை, ‘limit, boundary’) against tholl-ai (தொல்லை, ‘antiquity’): ellaikkan nindraar are those who stand within the limit (of friendship’s ethic), and thollaikkan nindraar are those who have stood with us from long ago. Tholaividaththum (தொலைவிடத்தும்) is read by most commentators as ‘even in loss or ruin’, from tholai- ‘to be destroyed’. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all take it as ‘even when the old friend’s acts bring harm’. Puliyur Kesigan reads it spatially, ‘even when they have gone to distant places’, and also takes thollai in its modern sense of ‘trouble’, giving ‘those who stood by us in our troubles’. The two readings change the image but keep the ethic of not abandoning old friends. Both base sources give the same text.

tamil:
அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார் அன்பின்
வழிவந்த கேண்மை யவர்.
transliteration:
Azhivandha seyyinum anbaraar anbin
vazhivandha kenmai yavar.
current_meaning: People whose friendship has grown through many years of love do not stop loving, even when their friends do things that cause them great harm.
elementary: Think of a very old tree with deep roots. A storm can break some branches, but the tree is still standing the next day. A friendship that has grown for years is like that: even a big hurt doesn’t pull it out of the ground.
university: Azhivandha (அழிவந்த) are ‘things that bring destruction’, and the concessive seyyinum (‘even if they do’) leads to anbaraar (அன்பறார், ‘they do not cut off love’). The subject is anbin vazhivandha kenmaiyavar, ‘those whose kenmai (கேண்மை, friendship) has come along the way of love’, which commentators take as long-standing, inherited affection. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as friendship come down ‘from of old’ (தொன்றுதொட்டு), and Solomon Pappaiah as long-standing friendship. Puliyur Kesigan alone shifts the subject, reading it as ‘our love for them will not be cut off’. The couplet is the strongest statement of the chapter’s ideal and has been criticised by modern readers as possibly encouraging tolerance of harm; the traditional commentators keep it within the framework of a tested, virtuous friendship (compare chapter 80). The text is identical in both base sources.

tamil:
கேளிழுக்கம் கேளாக் கெழுதகைமை வல்லார்க்கு
நாளிழுக்கம் நட்டார் செயின்.
transliteration:
Kelizhukkam kelaak kezhudhakaimai vallaarkku
naalizhukkam nattaar seyin.
current_meaning: Some people trust a close friend so much that they will not listen when others talk about that friend’s faults. For them, the day the friend really does wrong is a good day, because it proves their trust.
elementary: Someone at school whispers, ‘Your best friend said something mean about you.’ You say, ‘I don’t believe it.’ Later your friend really does make a mistake, and you work it out together. Your trust was strong enough to survive both the gossip and the mistake.
university: The couplet plays on repeated sounds: kel (கேள், ‘friend, kin’) + izhukkam (இழுக்கம், ‘fault’) is ‘a friend’s fault’, and kelaa (கேளா) is ‘not listening’. Its subject is the person vallaar (வல்லார், ‘skilled, strong’) in kezhudhakaimai who refuses to hear of a friend’s faults. The difficulty is naalizhukkam (நாளிழுக்கம்). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah, following the older interpretation, take the day the friend errs as a fruitful or useful day (பயனுள்ள நாள்) for such a person. Kalaignar reverses it: if friends wrong someone of such trust, all the days of that friendship are wasted. Puliyur Kesigan reads it as the friend’s fault seeming to be merely the fault of the day. G. U. Pope (‘The day his friend offends will day of grace to him appear’) follows the first reading. The text is the same in both base sources.

tamil:
கெடாஅ வழிவந்த கேண்மையார் கேண்மை
விடாஅர் விழையும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Kedaaa vazhivandha kenmaiyaar kenmai
vidaaar vizhaiyum ulagu.
current_meaning: The world loves people who never leave friends whose friendship has lasted, unbroken, for many years.
elementary: People trust the kid who has had the same best friend since kindergarten. If you stick with old friends, others think, ‘I would like a friend like that too.’
university: Kedaaa (கெடாஅ) and vidaaar (விடாஅர்) carry isai-nirai alapedai, a metrical lengthening that also adds emphasis: ‘never ruined’ and ‘never letting go’. Vazhivandha kenmaiyaar are ‘those whose friendship has come down along an unbroken path’. The main verb vizhaiyum ulagu, ‘the world desires or loves’, makes loyalty to old friends a source of public esteem. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read ‘the world praises’, while Puliyur Kesigan reads ‘everyone in the world will want such a person as a friend’. Solomon Pappaiah adds the qualification ‘even if the old friend does harm’, linking this couplet to 807. The text is the same in both base sources; the sandhi-split ytamizh form keeps the alapedai spellings.

tamil:
விழையார் விழையப் படுப பழையார்கண்
பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியா தார்.
transliteration:
Vizhaiyaar vizhaiyap paduba pazhaiyaarkan
panbin thalaippiriyaa thaar.
current_meaning: People who never lose their good feelings for old friends, even when those friends make mistakes, are loved even by their enemies.
elementary: There is a kid in class who is always loyal to friends, even when they mess up. Even the kids who don’t like them much have to admit, ‘Well, they’re a really good friend.’ Loyalty earns respect even from rivals.
university: Vizhaiyaar (விழையார், ‘those who do not wish one well’, i.e. enemies) becomes the agent of vizhaiyappaduba (‘are desired, loved’), a chiasmus: the unloving come to love. Pazhaiyaarkan (பழையார்கண்) is ‘toward old friends’, and panbin thalaippiriyaadhaar are ‘those who do not part from their disposition of goodwill’. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all supply ‘even though the friends do wrong’, carrying over the theme of 805-808. Puliyur Kesigan reads the reward as enemies wanting such a person as a friend. Closing the chapter with enemies’ esteem completes an arc from defining pazhaimai (801) to its social reward (809-810). Both base texts agree.

tamil:
பருகுவார் போலினும் பண்பிலார் கேண்மை
பெருகலிற் குன்றல் இனிது.
transliteration:
Parukuvaar poalinum panpilaar kenmai
perukalir kundral inidhu.
current_meaning: Even when people with bad character act so loving that they seem to want to drink you up, it is better for that friendship to shrink than to grow.
elementary: Some people hug you so tightly and say so many nice things that it feels wonderful. But if they are not kind or honest underneath, it is better to let that friendship get smaller instead of bigger, just like you would slowly back away from a puppy that wags its tail and also bites.
university: The chapter on tee natpu (தீ நட்பு, ‘evil friendship’) opens with its sharpest image: parukuvaar (பருகுவார்), ‘those who would drink you up’, describing a show of affection so intense it seems to swallow the friend whole. The defect is panpu-ilaar (பண்பிலார்), ‘those without good character’, so the warmth is not the test; character is. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both stress that the excess is appearance (‘தோன்றினாலும்’, ‘நடிக்கும்’), and Kalaignar speaks of being drowned in a flood of affection; all agree the right course is kundral (குன்றல்), letting the bond dwindle, rather than an abrupt break. This sets the chapter’s practical tone: Valluvar is less interested in condemning bad friends than in teaching how to reduce their hold. The text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net; the sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org prints ‘குன்ற லினிது’, a difference of word division only.

tamil:
உறின்நட்டு அறினொருஉம் ஒப்பிலார் கேண்மை
பெறினும் இழப்பினும் என்.
transliteration:
Urinnattu arinoruum oppilaar kenmai
perinum izhappinum en.
current_meaning: People who are not worth having as friends become close when they can get something and leave when they cannot. It makes no difference whether you gain or lose such friends.
elementary: Imagine a classmate who sits with you only on days you bring cookies, and walks away when you don’t. Having that ‘friend’ or not having them is really the same, because they were only ever friends with the cookies.
university: The couplet is built on two paired verbs: urin nattu (உறின் நட்டு), ‘when there is gain, befriending’, and arin oruum (அறின் ஒரூஉம்), ‘when it ends, departing’; ar- here means ‘to cease or be cut off’, and oruu is the lengthened (alapedai) form of ‘leave’. The subjects are oppilaar (ஒப்பிலார்), which Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan take as ‘the unworthy’ or ‘those of unequal nature’, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it with a twist, ‘those who have no equal in doing this’. The closing ‘en’ (என், ‘what of it?’) is a rhetorical shrug: such friendship is neither gain nor loss. Texts differ in spelling the second word: ytamizh has ‘அறினொருஉம்’, thirukkural.net prints ‘அறின்ஙருஉம்’ (apparently a typographic slip), and the sandhi-joined edition gives ‘உறினட் டறின்னொரூஉ’; the meaning is unaffected.

tamil:
உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் நட்பும் பெறுவது
கொள்வாரும் கள்வரும் நேர்.
transliteration:
Uruvadhu seerthookkum natpum peruvadhu
kolvaarum kalvarum ner.
current_meaning: A friend who weighs what they can get from you, a person who loves only for money, and a thief are all alike.
elementary: If someone is your friend only after checking what they can get from you, they are a bit like a person who takes things without asking. A real friend doesn’t keep a price list.
university: Valluvar sets three figures in a row and declares them ner (நேர், ‘equal’): the friend who does seerthookkal (சீர்தூக்கல், ‘weighing on a balance’) of uruvadhu (உறுவது, ‘what will come to him’); those who take only peruvadhu (பெறுவது, ‘what they receive’); and kalvar (கள்வர், ‘thieves’). The middle phrase, peruvadhu kolvaar, is read by Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesigan and Kalaignar, following the traditional gloss, as women who sell their company for payment; Solomon Pappaiah renders it as sex workers. The point is not to single anyone out but to define calculating friendship as a transaction for gain and to class it with taking what is not freely given. All three web texts agree on the wording; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘சீர்தூக்கு நட்பும்’ and ‘கள்வரு நேர்’, a matter of spelling convention.

tamil:
அமரகத்து ஆற்றறுக்கும் கல்லாமா அன்னார்
தமரின் தனிமை தலை.
transliteration:
Amarakaththu aatrarukkum kallaamaa annaar
thamarin thanimai thalai.
current_meaning: It is better to be alone than to have friends who are like an untrained horse that throws its rider off in the middle of a battle.
elementary: If you ride a bike with wobbly brakes, it might fail just when you’re going downhill. A friend who leaves you at the scariest moment is like that bike, and it’s safer to walk on your own.
university: The image is martial: amarakam (அமரகம்) is ‘the battlefield’, kallaa maa (கல்லா மா) ‘a horse that has not been trained’, and aatrarukkum (ஆற்றறுக்கும்) describes it cutting the rider off midway, whether by throwing him (Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar) or bolting from the field (Puliyur Kesigan, who widens maa to ‘an untaught beast’). Thamar (தமர்) means ‘one’s own people, intimates’, and the verdict is thanimai thalai (தனிமை தலை): solitude is supreme. The couplet sharpens the chapter’s logic: a bad friend is not merely useless but dangerous at exactly the moment you depend on him. The texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘அமரகத் தாற்றறுக்குங் கல்லாமா வன்னார் தமரிற் றனிமை தலை’.

tamil:
செய்தேமஞ் சாராச் சிறியவர் புன்கேண்மை
எய்தலின் எய்தாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Seydhemanj saaraach chiriyavar punkenmai
eydhalin eydhaamai nandru.
current_meaning: Small-minded people will not protect you, even after you have done a lot for them. It is better never to have their poor friendship than to have it.
elementary: Think of an umbrella with holes in it. You can carry it, take care of it and open it every time, but it still won’t keep you dry. Some friends are like that, and it’s better not to count on them at all.
university: The key compound is seydhemam saaraa (செய்தேமம் சாரா): ēmam (ஏமம்) is ‘protection, safety’, and the phrase means ‘not coming to be a protection even when it has been made one’. Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as ‘though set to guard, they do not guard’, Solomon Pappaiah as ‘though we help them in many ways, they are no protection to us’, and Puliyur Kesigan as ‘they do not come to rescue us when trouble arrives’. Chiriyavar (சிறியவர்) are ‘the small’, people mean in mind, and their bond is pun-kenmai (புன்கேண்மை), ‘paltry friendship’. The conclusion, eydhalin eydhaamai nandru, ‘not attaining is better than attaining’, extends 814: such friendship is not neutral but a net loss. The text is uniform across the three sources, the sandhi-joined edition writing ‘யெய்தலி னெய்தாமை’.

tamil:
பேதை பெருங்கெழீஇ நட்பின் அறிவுடையார்
ஏதின்மை கோடி உறும்.
transliteration:
Pedhai perungezheei natpin arivudaiyaar
edhinmai kodi urum.
current_meaning: Being a stranger, or even an enemy, to wise people is worth ten million times more than being a very close friend of a fool.
elementary: If you’re building a sandcastle, a careful kid who doesn’t like you will still not knock it over, but a clumsy best friend might jump right on it while trying to help. Sometimes a sensible rival is safer than a silly friend.
university: The couplet sets pedhai perung kezheei natpu (பேதை பெருங்கெழீஇ நட்பு), ‘the greatly intimate friendship of a fool’, against arivudaiyaar edhinmai (அறிவுடையார் ஏதின்மை), and the reading of edhinmai divides commentators. Edhilaar means ‘strangers, outsiders’, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan take edhinmai as ‘the absence of friendship’, being unconnected to the wise; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar sharpen it to ‘enmity’ (பகை), giving the more striking proverb ‘a wise enemy is better than a foolish friend’. Kezheei (கெழீஇ) is the alapedai form of kezhu-, ‘to be closely joined’. ‘Kodi urum’ (கோடி உறும்) means ‘is worth a crore’, i.e., ten million times over. The texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘நட்பி னறிவுடையா ரேதின்மை’.

tamil:
நகைவகைய ராகிய நட்பின் பகைவரால்
பத்தடுத்த கோடி உறும்.
transliteration:
Nakaivakaiya raakiya natpin pakaivaraal
paththaduththa kodi urum.
current_meaning: What you get from your enemies is worth a hundred million times more than the friendship of people who only laugh along with you.
elementary: A friend who just giggles at everything never tells you there’s spinach in your teeth. Even someone who doesn’t like you might point it out. Sometimes honest criticism helps more than easy laughter.
university: Nakaivakaiyar (நகைவகையர்) are ‘those of the laughing kind’: Mu. Varadarasanar adds ‘laughing outwardly without love within’, Kalaignar ‘those who laugh and talk as a performance’, and Puliyur Kesigan ‘those useful only for idle talk and merriment’. Against them stands what comes from pakaivar (பகைவர், ‘enemies’), worth paththaduththa kodi (பத்தடுத்த கோடி), ‘ten crore’ or a hundred million times more. The exaggeration escalates the kodi of 816. Commentators differ on what an enemy provides: most modern glosses say ‘benefit’, while Kalaignar paradoxically says even the suffering enemies cause is worth more, because it at least makes one alert. The wording agrees across ytamizh and thirukkural.net; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘நட்பிற் பகைவராற்’.

tamil:
ஒல்லும் கருமம் உடற்று பவர்கேண்மை
சொல்லாடார் சோர விடல்.
transliteration:
Ollum karumam udatru pavarkenmai
sollaadaar sora vidal.
current_meaning: Some people pretend they cannot help and so spoil a job that could easily be done. Let your friendship with them quietly fade without saying anything.
elementary: If a friend always says ‘I can’t’ whenever you need a small hand, even when they easily could, you don’t need to have a big fight. You can just slowly spend more time with friends who do help.
university: Ollum karumam (ஒல்லும் கருமம்) is ‘a task that can be done’; udatrupavar (உடற்றுபவர்) are those who ‘harass’ or ruin it, which Solomon Pappaiah and the classical English versions read as feigning inability to do what they could, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar as making the possible impossible. The remedy is notably mild: sollaadaar (சொல்லாடார்), ‘without speaking of it’, sora vidal (சோர விடல்), ‘let it slacken’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read sollaadaar as ‘without letting them know’, Puliyur Kesigan as ‘by ceasing to talk with them’. The counsel is gradual disengagement rather than confrontation, a tactful way to avoid making a fresh enemy. The texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘ஒல்லுங் கரும முடற்று பவர்கேண்மை’.

tamil:
கனவினும் இன்னாது மன்னோ வினைவேறு
சொல்வேறு பட்டார் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Kanavinum innaadhu manno vinaiveru
solveru pattaar thodarpu.
current_meaning: Friendship with people whose actions and words do not match hurts you even in a dream.
elementary: If a friend promises to save you a seat and then gives it to someone else, and does it again and again, you start feeling uneasy even when you’re just thinking about them. A friend’s words and actions should match.
university: The couplet names the fault precisely: vinai veru, sol veru (வினை வேறு, சொல் வேறு), ‘deed apart, word apart’, the divorce of action from speech. Kanavinum (கனவினும், ‘even in a dream’) intensifies: such a connection hurts not only in waking life, as Puliyur Kesigan spells out, but even in sleep. Manno (மன்னோ) is an emotive particle of emphasis or lament, which Sivayogi Sivakumar renders as a rhetorical question, ‘will it not give pain even in a dream?’ The word here is thodarpu (தொடர்பு, ‘connection, association’) rather than natpu, perhaps suggesting such people never achieve true friendship. All three texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition prints ‘கனவினு மின்னாது’.

tamil:
எனைத்தும் குறுகுதல் ஓம்பல் மனைக்கெழீஇ
மன்றில் பழிப்பார் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Enaiththum kurukudhal ombal manaikkezheei
mandril pazhippaar thodarpu.
current_meaning: Do not get even a little close to people who are friendly with you in private but say bad things about you in public.
elementary: Imagine someone who plays nicely with you at your house but makes fun of you in front of the whole class. That’s not a real friend, and it’s wise to keep your distance from them.
university: The chapter closes on the double-faced friend: manaik kezheei (மனைக் கெழீஇ), ‘intimate in the house’, and mandril pazhippaar (மன்றில் பழிப்பார்), ‘those who revile in the manram’, the public hall or assembly where reputations are made. The prescription is the strongest in the chapter: enaiththum kurukudhal ombal (எனைத்தும் குறுகுதல் ஓம்பல்), ‘guard against approaching in any measure at all’. Where 811 and 818 allowed a gradual waning, here even the slightest contact is to be avoided, since such a person turns private trust into public damage. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesigan all read manai literally as ‘home’, while Kalaignar’s gloss refers to private moments. The texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘எனைத்துங் குறுகுத லோம்பன்’ and ‘மன்றிற் பழிப்பார்’.

tamil:
சீரிடம் காணின் எறிதற்குப் பட்டடை
நேரா நிரந்தவர் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Seeridam kaanin erithar̲kup pattadai
neraa niranthavar natpu.
current_meaning: The friendship of people who spend time with you but are not with you in heart is like an anvil, the iron block a blacksmith hammers on. When the time is right, they will strike you down on it.
elementary: A blacksmith’s anvil looks like a strong, steady table, but its real job is to hold the metal still so the hammer can hit it. A fake friend can feel like solid support, but they are only holding you in place until it suits them to let you get hurt.
university: The chapter title kooḍaa naṭpu (கூடா நட்பு) means ‘friendship that does not truly join’, and this opening couplet defines it: those who are neraa (நேரா, not inwardly agreeing) yet niranthavar (நிரந்தவர், outwardly close). Paṭṭaḍai (பட்டடை) is the smith’s anvil, the block on which metal is laid to be cut; Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read the simile this way, Pappaiah adding that it looks like support while really serving the cutting. Seer-idam (சீரிடம்) is ‘the fitting place or occasion’, so the danger lies in timing: the false friend waits for an opening. Parimelazhagar places this chapter after Thee Natpu (82, evil friendship) as a treatment of friendship that is enmity in disguise, a theme he reads in a royal-political frame. The couplet is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இனம்போன்று இனமல்லார் கேண்மை மகளிர்
மனம்போல வேறு படும்.
transliteration:
Inampondru inamallaar kenmai magalir
manampola veru padum.
current_meaning: The friendship of people who act like your own family but are not will keep changing, like the heart of someone whose love depends on being paid.
elementary: Some kids are your friend only when you have the best snack at lunch. The day you have nothing to share, they sit somewhere else. Their friendship changes shape depending on what they can get.
university: Inam (இனம்) means one’s own circle or kin; inam-pondru inam-allaar are those who resemble kin but are not. Kenmai (கேண்மை) is intimacy or friendship. The comparison with magalir manam (மகளிர் மனம்) is read by Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar, Puliyur Kesigan) specifically as the mind of courtesans (பொதுமகளிர் / விலைமகளிர்), whose affection follows payment, not as a judgment on women in general; Puliyur Kesigan glosses the point as changing ‘according to the gain received’. The comparison reflects the social assumptions of its age, but its logical point is clear: an attachment driven by gain changes when the gain changes. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்து மனநல்லர்
ஆகுதல் மாணார்க் கரிது.
transliteration:
Palanalla kat̲rak kadaiththu mananallar
aaguthal maanaark karithu.
current_meaning: Even after studying many good books, people with a bad nature find it hard to become good at heart.
elementary: You can read every book about kindness and still be unkind. Knowing the rules of a game does not make you a fair player. A person who doesn’t care about you can learn lots of nice words without their heart changing.
university: Pala nalla katrak kadaiththu (பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்து) means ‘even when it happens that they have learned many good things’; mana-nallar (மனநல்லர்) are the good-hearted. Maanaar (மாணார்) literally means ‘those who are not excellent’; Varadarasanar glosses it as those who have not attained greatness through inner affection, while Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as those hostile at heart (பகையுணர்வு படைத்தோர்), and Pope’s gloss ‘enemies’ follows the latter. The couplet thus warns against assuming that a learned enemy has been softened by learning: knowledge of virtue is not virtue. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா
வஞ்சரை அஞ்சப் படும்.
transliteration:
Mugaththin iniya nagaaa agaththinnaa
vanjarai anjap padum.
current_meaning: Watch out for tricksters who smile sweetly with their faces while their hearts are bitter toward you.
elementary: A shiny red apple can still have a worm inside. A big smile on the outside does not always mean kindness on the inside, so it is wise to watch what people do, not just how they smile.
university: The couplet sets mugam (முகம், face) against agam (அகம், the inner self), a pairing that will return in Kural 830. Nagaaa (நகாஅ, ‘smiling’) shows alapeḍai, the metrical lengthening of a vowel, and akaththinnaa (அகத்து இன்னா) means ‘bitter or harmful within’. Vanjar (வஞ்சர்) are deceivers, and anjappaḍum (அஞ்சப்படும்) is the impersonal ‘is to be feared’; Varadarasanar reads it as fearing to make friends with them, Kalaignar as fearing them and keeping away. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மனத்தின் அமையா தவரை எனைத்தொன்றும்
சொல்லினால் தேறற்பாற்று அன்று.
transliteration:
Manaththin amaiyaa thavarai enaiththondrum
sollinaal ther̲ar̲paat̲ru andru.
current_meaning: Never trust, in anything at all, the words of people who are not with you in their hearts.
elementary: If someone keeps promising to share their toys but never does, you learn to stop believing the promise. Words are easy to say. When someone does not really care about you, what they say is not something to lean on.
university: Manaththin amaiyaathavar (மனத்தின் அமையாதவர்) are ‘those not settled with us in mind’; enaiththondrum (எனைத்தொன்றும்) means ‘in anything at all’. Theraṟpaaṯru anru (தேறற்பாற்று அன்று) means ‘it is not fit to be trusted or relied upon’, using theṟal (தேறல், clear conviction), the same root as the chapter Therindhu Thelidhal (51) on testing before trusting. Varadarasanar reads it as not trusting their words in any undertaking, and Kalaignar as not being able to reach any clear decision on such people’s words. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நட்டார்போல் நல்லவை சொல்லினும் ஒட்டார்சொல்
ஒல்லை உணரப் படும்.
transliteration:
Nattaarpol nallavai sollinum ottaarsol
ollai unarap padum.
current_meaning: Even when enemies say good things as if they were friends, people soon see what their words really mean.
elementary: A wolf can try to sound like a sheep, but sooner or later it growls. When someone who doesn’t like you starts talking sweetly, listen carefully; the truth usually shows up quickly.
university: Naṭṭaar (நட்டார்) are friends, those who have made friendship, and oṭṭaar (ஒட்டார்) are those who do not ‘stick’ or join with us, that is, foes. Nallavai sollinum (நல்லவை சொல்லினும்) concedes that the words themselves may be good, and ollai (ஒல்லை) means ‘quickly’. The couplet is partly reassurance: false friendship tends to betray itself in speech, and Kalaignar says the meanness in such words will come out without fail. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read the ‘understanding’ as recognising quickly that the words are not truly meant for our good. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
சொல்வணக்கம் ஒன்னார்கண் கொள்ளற்க வில்வணக்கம்
தீங்கு குறித்தமை யான்.
transliteration:
Solvanakkam onnaarkan kollar̲ka vilvanakkam
theengu kur̲iththamai yaan.
current_meaning: Do not trust an enemy’s polite, bowing words. A bow bends low only so it can shoot and do harm.
elementary: When an archer pulls back a bow, it bends down low, almost like it is bowing politely. But that bend is what sends the arrow flying. Sometimes people who don’t like you act extra polite right before they try to hurt you.
university: The couplet turns on a pun in vaṇakkam (வணக்கம்), which means both ‘bowing, reverence’ and ‘bending’: sol-vaṇakkam is ‘humility in speech’, vil-vaṇakkam ‘the bending of a bow’. Onnaar (ஒன்னார்) are those who are not one with us, enemies. Since the bow’s bend ‘signals harm’ (theengu kuṟiththamaiyaan, தீங்கு குறித்தமையான்), a foe’s deferential words should be read the same way; Pappaiah and Kalaignar draw out the simile in this sense, and Pope translates ‘pliant speech’ and ‘pliant bow’. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும் ஒன்னார்
அழுதகண் ணீரும் அனைத்து.
transliteration:
Thozhuthagai yullum padaiyodungum onnaar
azhuthagan neerum anaiththu.
current_meaning: An enemy may hide a weapon in the hands they fold before you in respect. Their tears hide harm in the same way.
elementary: Imagine someone bowing to you with hands pressed together, but hiding a water balloon behind them. Pretend sadness can be a trick too. If someone has been mean to you, a show of respect or tears doesn’t always mean they have changed.
university: Thozhuthagai (தொழுதகை) is the hand joined in worship or salutation, and paḍai oḍungum (படை ஒடுங்கும்) means ‘a weapon lies concealed’. The second line extends the image: onnaar azhutha kaṇṇeer (ஒன்னார் அழுத கண்ணீர், the tears foes have wept) is anaiththu (அனைத்து, of that same kind). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read the couplet literally as a weapon concealed in the worshipping hand, and Kalaignar adds that even in weeping their hearts are full of plotting. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; thirukkural.net prints the words as தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் and கண் ணீரும் with the same metrical division.

tamil:
மிகச்செய்து தம்மெள்ளு வாரை நகச்செய்து
நட்பினுள் சாப்புல்லற் பாற்று.
transliteration:
Migachcheythu thammellu vaarai nagachcheythu
natpinul saappullar̲ paat̲ru.
current_meaning: When people make a big show of friendship but secretly look down on you, smile back at them on the outside, but let that friendship die inside you.
elementary: If a classmate is super-friendly to your face but laughs at you behind your back, you don’t have to start a fight. You can stay polite and friendly when you meet, but quietly stop trusting them and stop sharing your secrets.
university: Migachcheythu (மிகச்செய்து) is ‘making much of (friendship)’, and thammeḷḷuvaar (தம் எள்ளுவார்) are ‘those who scorn us’ within. The difficult phrase saappullaṟpaaṯru (சாப்புல்லற்பாற்று) is read by the commentators as ‘one should embrace (pullal) in such a way that it dies (saa)’: Varadarasanar says one should make them laugh in that friendship while acting so that the bond dies, and Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as answering pretence with pretence. Pope’s explanation, in the tradition of Parimelazhagar’s royal-political reading, presents this as the duty of kings toward such foes. Whether read as defensive policy or as cynicism, the couplet assumes a political setting where open rupture is costly; ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give identical text.

tamil:
பகைநட்பாம் காலம் வருங்கால் முகநட்டு
அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல்.
transliteration:
Paganatpaam kaalam varungaal muganattu
aganatpu oreei vidal.
current_meaning: When the time comes that you must treat an enemy like a friend, be friendly on your face but keep them out of your heart, and drop them when you can.
elementary: Sometimes you have to work on a group project with someone who has been unkind to you. You can be polite and work together, but you don’t have to hand them your diary. Be friendly on the outside and careful on the inside.
university: Pagai-naṭpaam kaalam (பகை நட்பாம் காலம்) is ‘a time when enmity turns into friendship’, for instance an alliance forced by circumstances. The couplet resolves the chapter with the face/heart pair already used in Kural 824: muga-naṭṭu (முகநட்டு, befriending with the face) but aga-naṭpu oreei (அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ, removing friendship from the heart). Oreei (ஒரீஇ) is the alapeḍai-lengthened form of oree, ‘leaving’, and viḍal (விடல்) means ‘one should give it up’. Varadarasanar reads the final word as giving up even the outward friendship when the chance comes, Pappaiah as letting go of it in the mind, and Pope follows the first reading with ‘give up (even the former)’. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பேதைமை என்பதொன்று யாதெனின் ஏதங்கொண்டு
ஊதியம் போக விடல்.
transliteration:
Pedhaimai enbadhondru yaadhenin edhangkondu
oodhiyam poga vidal.
current_meaning: What is foolishness? It is grabbing what hurts you and letting go of what would help you.
elementary: Imagine someone offers you a choice between a shiny toy that will break in a day and a bicycle you could ride for years, and you pick the toy and walk away from the bike. That swap, keeping the bad thing and dropping the good one, is exactly what the poet calls being foolish.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition rather than an example: pedhaimai (பேதைமை) is the act of taking up edham (ஏதம், harm, loss) and letting oodhiyam (ஊதியம், gain, profit) go. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read the pair as a ledger of consequences: the fool does not merely fail to gain, he actively trades gain for loss, which is why folly is placed in the Natpiyal section right after the chapters on bad friendship. Puliyur Kesigan sharpens this into a cost-benefit reading (accepting the trouble that comes with a task while throwing away the profit it would bring), whereas Sivayogi Sivakumar reads edhangkondu as ‘out of fear of a small hardship’, a softer psychological gloss. Kalaignar stresses the failure of discernment: the fool never clarifies which is harmful and which is beneficial. The text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பேதைமையுள் எல்லாம் பேதைமை காதன்மை
கையல்ல தன்கட் செயல்.
transliteration:
Pedhaimaiyul ellaam pedhaimai kaadhanmai
kaiyalla thankat seyal.
current_meaning: The worst foolishness of all is wanting to do things you should not do.
elementary: A goldfish might dream of climbing trees like a squirrel, but if it jumps out of its bowl to try, it will only get hurt. The silliest mistake is wanting badly to do things that are not right for who you are.
university: The couplet ranks follies and puts at the top kaadhanmai (காதன்மை, fond desire, love) for kaiyalla (கையல்ல, what is not within one’s proper hand or conduct). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take kaiyalla as acts unsuited to one’s own moral conduct (ஒழுக்கம்), which matches G. U. Pope’s ‘deeds which to your station unbefitting prove’ and Drew’s ‘delight in doing what is forbidden’. Kalaignar instead reads it as deeds beyond one’s ability, Solomon Pappaiah as desiring things that do one no good, and Puliyur Kesigan as both choosing an undesirable act and doing it unfittingly; the line thus spans a moral reading (forbidden) and a prudential one (beyond one’s scope). The wording is the same in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நாணாமை நாடாமை நாரின்மை யாதொன்றும்
பேணாமை பேதை தொழில்.
transliteration:
Naanaamai naadaamai naarinmai yaadhondrum
penaamai pedhai thozhil.
current_meaning: Feeling no shame, not looking for what is worth having, having no love, and caring about nothing: these are the habits of a fool.
elementary: Think of a kid who breaks a window and doesn’t feel sorry, never tries to learn anything, isn’t kind to friends, and leaves their toys out in the rain. Each of those things on its own is a warning sign; together they are what the poet calls a fool.
university: The couplet is a fourfold catalogue built on negative nouns ending in -aamai/-inmai: naanaamai (நாணாமை, shamelessness at what deserves shame), naadaamai (நாடாமை, not seeking out what deserves seeking), naarinmai (நாரின்மை, lack of naar, ‘fibre’, a metaphor for the affection that binds people), and penaamai (பேணாமை, not cherishing or protecting anything). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar gloss naar as anbu (love), and the commentators agree the list describes a whole disposition rather than isolated faults; Pope renders it ‘Ashamed of nothing, searching nothing out, of loveless heart, / Nought cherishing’. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads naarinmai as lacking sweetness of manner, a minor variation. The text is identical in both base sources.

tamil:
ஓதி உணர்ந்தும் பிறர்க்குரைத்தும் தானடங்காப்
பேதையின் பேதையார் இல்.
transliteration:
Odhi unarndhum pirarkkuraiththum thaanadangaap
pedhaiyin pedhaiyaar il.
current_meaning: No one is a bigger fool than someone who has studied, understood, and even taught others, yet does not live by what they learned.
elementary: Imagine a swimming coach who teaches everyone how to stay safe in the pool but then jumps into the deep end without looking. Knowing the rules and telling others is not enough; the biggest silliness is not following them yourself.
university: The couplet climbs three steps, odhi (ஓதி, having recited or studied), unarndhum (உணர்ந்தும், having understood) and pirarkku uraiththum (பிறர்க்கு உரைத்தும், having explained to others), and then collapses on thaan adangaa (தான் அடங்கா, himself not restrained, not conforming). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take adangudhal as living within the discipline the texts teach, and the superlative pedhaiyin pedhaiyaar il (‘there is no fool beyond this fool’) makes the learned hypocrite the extreme case of the chapter. Puliyur Kesigan glosses adangaa as lacking self-restraint (adakkam), linking the couplet to the chapter on Adakkamudaimai. All four commentaries and the two base texts agree on the reading.

tamil:
ஒருமைச் செயலாற்றும் பேதை எழுமையும்
தான்புக் கழுந்தும் அளறு.
transliteration:
Orumaich cheyalaatrum pedhai ezhumaiyum
thaanpuk kazhundhum alaru.
current_meaning: In just one life, a fool can do enough wrong to fall into a hell of suffering that lasts through seven future lives.
elementary: A few minutes of scribbling with permanent marker on your bedroom wall can leave a mess that takes weeks to clean. The poet says the foolish person can make, in one life, a mess so big it sticks to him for a very long time.
university: The couplet sets orumai (ஒருமை, one birth) against ezhumai (எழுமை, the seven births), and alaru (அளறு, literally ‘mire’ or ‘mud’) is the traditional word for naragam, hell. Parimelazhagar, Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah all read it eschatologically: in one life the fool is able to make (ஆற்றும்) the hell he will enter and sink into across seven births. Kalaignar departs from this, reading orumaich cheyal as ‘self-willed action’ and alaru as a mire of suffering in this world, a deliberately non-theological gloss; Puliyur Kesigan’s note on thirukkural.net is truncated. Pope’s ‘The fool will merit hell in one brief life on earth’ follows the traditional reading. The text is the same in both base sources.

tamil:
பொய்படும் ஒன்றோ புனைபூணும் கையறியாப்
பேதை வினைமேற் கொளின்.
transliteration:
Poipadum ondro punaipoonum kaiyariyaap
pedhai vinaimer kolin.
current_meaning: When a fool takes on a job they do not know how to do, the job fails, and they also end up in chains.
elementary: If someone who has never cooked tries to make a big dinner alone, the food gets burnt, and they might also burn their hand. Taking on a job you don’t know how to do can spoil the job and hurt you too.
university: Kaiyariyaa (கையறியா) means ‘not knowing the method’ (kai here is the way of doing), and the couplet’s rhetorical ondro (ஒன்றோ, ‘is it only one thing?’) introduces a double penalty: the work poipadum (பொய்படும், comes to nothing) and the doer punai poonum (புனைபூணும், wears fetters). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan take punai literally as the shackles of a man held culpable, which Pope follows (‘himself he binds with chains’), while Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar soften it to ‘he too is ruined’ or ‘punishes himself’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss kaiyariyaa morally (not knowing the right way of conduct), whereas Pappaiah reads it practically (not knowing how to do the work). Both base sources give the same text.

tamil:
ஏதிலார் ஆரத் தமர்பசிப்பர் பேதை
பெருஞ்செல்வம் உற்றக் கடை.
transliteration:
Edhilaar aarath thamarpasippar pedhai
perunjelvam utrak kadai.
current_meaning: When a fool becomes very rich, strangers enjoy that money while the fool's own family goes hungry.
elementary: Imagine a boy who wins a huge bag of candy and hands it all out to kids he barely knows, while his little sister at home gets none. Having lots of something doesn’t help your family if you don’t know how to share it wisely.
university: The couplet contrasts edhilaar (ஏதிலார், strangers, those with no tie) who aara (ஆர, eat their fill) with thamar (தமர், one’s own kin) who pasippar (பசிப்பர், go hungry). Puliyur Kesigan follows the traditional explanation that the fool’s wealth comes from past merit (munvinai), while the lack of judgment in spending it is his own; Parimelazhagar’s tradition reads the strangers as flatterers and parasites who gather round new wealth. Kalaignar’s gloss stresses that outsiders ‘roll up’ the money while affectionate kin go without. Pope renders edhilaar as ‘foes’, a stronger word than the Tamil requires; Drew’s ‘neighbours’ is closer. The text is the same in both base sources.

tamil:
மையல் ஒருவன் களித்தற்றால் பேதைதன்
கையொன்று உடைமை பெறின்.
transliteration:
Maiyal oruvan kaliththatraal pedhaidhan
kaiyondru udaimai perin.
current_meaning: When a fool gets hold of something valuable, they are like a person who is already out of their mind and then gets drunk too.
elementary: Picture a kid who is already running wild at a party and then gets a big bag of sugar. Things go from silly to much worse! Giving power or money to someone who doesn’t think clearly only makes their foolishness bigger.
university: The simile doubles the condition: maiyal (மையல், bewilderment, madness) is a man already deranged, and kaliththal (களித்தல்) is intoxication by toddy, so the fool who gains udaimai (உடைமை, possession) is a madman who is also drunk. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss maiyal as piththu (பித்து, madness) and kaliththal as being dazed by kal (கள், toddy), and Puliyur Kesigan adds that such a man drinks more and more and strays from his course. Kai ondru (கை ஒன்று) is read as ‘anything in his hand’, so the point holds for any wealth or authority, not only great fortune. Pope (‘as when a mad man raves in drunken glee’) and Drew follow the same reading, and the two base sources agree on the text.

tamil:
பெரிதினிது பேதையார் கேண்மை பிரிவின்கண்
பீழை தருவதொன் றில்.
transliteration:
Peridhinidhu pedhaiyaar kenmai pirivinkan
peezhai tharuvadhon ril.
current_meaning: Friendship with fools is very sweet, because when it ends, saying goodbye causes no pain at all.
elementary: Some friends are like a balloon on a string: it is fun for a while, but when it floats away you don’t really miss it. The poet is joking that friends who are foolish are ‘lovely’, because losing them doesn’t hurt at all.
university: The couplet is ironic praise: peridhu inidhu (பெரிது இனிது, ‘exceedingly sweet’) is applied to pedhaiyaar kenmai (பேதையார் கேண்மை, friendship with fools), and the reason given is that at pirivu (பிரிவு, separation) there is no peezhai (பீழை, pain, affliction). Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesigan all read it as saying that a fool’s friendship is ‘sweet’ only in that losing it costs nothing, so its real worth is zero; Kesigan hedges with ‘in one way’. Solomon Pappaiah reads it slightly differently, as friendship among fools themselves, whose partings cause them no grief, which matches Drew’s ‘the friendship between fools’. The text is the same in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கழாஅக்கால் பள்ளியுள் வைத்தற்றால் சான்றோர்
குழாஅத்துப் பேதை புகல்.
transliteration:
Kazhaaakkaal palliyul vaiththatraal saandror
kuzhaaaththup pedhai pugal.
current_meaning: A fool walking into a meeting of wise people is like putting dirty feet on a clean bed.
elementary: Imagine coming in from a muddy football field and climbing straight into a freshly made bed with dirty feet. Everything gets messy. The poet says a fool barging into a group of wise people spoils things in the same way.
university: The closing simile sets kazhaaak kaal (கழாஅக்கால், unwashed foot) in palli (பள்ளி) against the fool’s pugal (புகல், entering) into saandror kuzhaaam (சான்றோர் குழாஅம், the gathering of the noble). The lengthened forms kazhaaa- and kuzhaaa- are isai-nirai alapedai (இசைநிறை அளபெடை), vowel prolongation that fills out the metre. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take palli as a bed (as do Pope and Drew), but Puliyur Kesigan reads it as a place of worship (‘தொழுகைக்குரிய பள்ளி’), making the image one of defiling a sanctuary; both senses of palli are attested in Tamil. The text is identical in both base sources.

tamil:
அறிவின்மை இன்மையுள் இன்மை பிறிதின்மை
இன்மையா வையா துலகு.
transliteration:
Arivinmai inmaiyul inmai piridhinmai
inmaiyaa vaiyaa thulagu.
current_meaning: Of all the things a person can lack, lacking good sense is the real poverty. The world does not count lacking other things, like money, as real poverty.
elementary: Imagine two kids: one has an empty piggy bank but knows how to read, count and solve problems; the other has a full piggy bank but can’t figure anything out. The first one can earn coins again, but the second one will keep losing them. That is why the poet says not knowing is the emptiest pocket of all.
university: The chapter opens with a paradox built on the repeated word inmai (இன்மை, lack, poverty): arivinmai (அறிவின்மை, absence of understanding) is ‘the poverty among poverties’, while piridhinmai (other lacks, chiefly of wealth) the world will not reckon as poverty at all. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar render it as ‘the famine of knowledge is the cruelest famine’, and Solomon Pappaiah shifts the evaluator from ‘the world’ (ulagu) to ‘the great ones’ (periyor), reflecting the classical commentary habit of reading ulagu as ‘the wise of the world’. Puliyur Kesigan adds that material poverty is not regarded as lasting poverty, since it can be remedied, whereas folly cannot. Placed in the Natpiyal after Pedhaimai (ch. 84), Pullarivaanmai shifts the focus from simple folly to the conceited, perverse ignorance (pull-arivu, ‘petty knowledge’) of one who thinks himself wise. Text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the second line is printed in its traditional sandhi-split form ‘inmaiyaa vaiyaa thulagu’ (for vaiyaadhu ulagu).

tamil:
அறிவிலான் நெஞ்சுவந்து ஈதல் பிறிதியாதும்
இல்லை பெறுவான் தவம்.
transliteration:
Arivilaan nenjuvandhu eedhal piridhiyaadhum
illai peruvaan thavam.
current_meaning: When a fool happily gives something away, it is only because of the good luck the receiver earned from past good deeds.
elementary: Suppose a kid who never shares suddenly hands you his best sandwich with a big smile. You didn’t earn it from his good sense; you were just lucky that day. The poet says a fool’s gift is like that: it comes from the receiver’s good luck, not the giver’s wisdom.
university: The kural is ironic: a person without understanding (arivilaan, அறிவிலான்) does not give wisely, so if he gives nenjuvandhu (நெஞ்சுவந்து, with a gladdened heart), the explanation must lie outside him, in the thavam (தவம், austerity, accumulated merit) of the recipient (peruvaan). Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah gloss thavam as nalvinai (good karma), and the old English rendering speaks of ‘the receiver’s merit (in a former birth)’, reflecting the karmic reading of the classical commentators. Kalaignar softens it to ‘the receiver’s good fortune’, while Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as the receiver’s own spiritual quality drawing the gift. The underlying point is that the fool’s generosity is unreliable and unearned, an accident of providence rather than a virtue. No textual variants appear between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அறிவிலார் தாந்தம்மைப் பீழிக்கும் பீழை
செறுவார்க்கும் செய்தல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Arivilaar thaandhammaip peezhikkum peezhai
seruvaarkkum seydhal aridhu.
current_meaning: Fools bring more suffering on themselves than even their enemies could cause them.
elementary: Think of a kid who won’t wear a coat in the snow, eats all the candy at once and then skips homework. No bully could make his day as miserable as he has made it himself. The poet says fools are their own worst enemies.
university: Valluvar uses the doubled noun-verb peezhikkum peezhai (பீழிக்கும் பீழை, the affliction with which they afflict) to stress self-made misery, and seruvaar (செறுவார், those who hate, enemies) to set up the comparison. All the modern commentators agree on the sense: the harm fools do to themselves exceeds what an enemy could achieve (Mu. Varadarasanar: ‘of a measure even their foes cannot inflict’; Kalaignar: ‘the torment enemies could not deliver, fools give themselves’). Puliyur Kesigan notes the distress-causing nature (varuththam) of such self-inflicted suffering. The thought links this chapter to the Natpiyal’s concern with enemies: for the fool, the most dangerous enemy is internal. Both web texts read identically.

tamil:
வெண்மை எனப்படுவ தியாதெனின் ஒண்மை
உடையம்யாம் என்னும் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Venmai enappaduva dhiyaadhenin onmai
udaiyamyaam ennum serukku.
current_meaning: What is stupidity? It is the proud belief that says, “We are the wise ones.”
elementary: A kid who says “I already know everything, I don’t need to listen” stops learning right there. The poet says that feeling of being sure you are the smartest is exactly what being foolish means.
university: The kural defines folly by a pair of light-words: venmai (வெண்மை, literally ‘whiteness’, i.e. blankness, emptiness of mind) is set against onmai (ஒண்மை, ‘brightness’, i.e. keen intelligence). Folly is not mere blankness but the serukku (செருக்கு, conceit, intoxicated pride) that claims brightness: ‘udaiyam yaam’, ‘we possess it’, with the royal or self-inflating plural. Mu. Varadarasanar equates venmai with pullarivu, the chapter’s key term; Pappaiah calls it a ‘delusion’ (mayakkam) and Kalaignar ‘arrogance’ (aanavam). Structurally the kural mirrors 831 in the preceding chapter (‘pedhaimai enbadhondru yaadhenin…’), giving a definition in question-and-answer form. Text identical in both sources.

tamil:
கல்லாத மேற்கொண் டொழுகல் கசடற
வல்லதூஉம் ஐயம் தரும்.
transliteration:
Kallaadha merkon dozhugal kasadara
valladhooum aiyam tharum.
current_meaning: Pretending to know things you never learned makes people doubt even the things you really do know well.
elementary: If a boy who is great at football starts bragging that he is also a chess champion, and everyone sees he can’t play chess, they start wondering whether he is really good at football either. Faking one thing makes people doubt the real things too.
university: Kallaadha (கல்லாத, what one has not learned) set against kasadara valladhu (கசடற வல்லது, what one has mastered without flaw) gives the kural its hinge, and the emphatic -ooum (‘even that’) shows the reach of the damage: aiyam (ஐயம், doubt) spreads from the pretended to the genuine. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read kallaadha as unread books (nool), so the fool pretends to scholarship; Kalaignar widens it to any field one pretends to know. Puliyur Kesigan reads merkondu ozhugal more actively as rashly undertaking a task one has not learned, which casts doubt even on work one could do perfectly. The kural is a pointed observation about credibility: a single exposed pretense devalues an entire reputation. Both sources give identical text.

tamil:
அற்றம் மறைத்தலோ புல்லறிவு தம்வயின்
குற்றம் மறையா வழி.
transliteration:
Atram maraiththalo pullarivu thamvayin
kutram maraiyaa vazhi.
current_meaning: If you do not get rid of your faults, then carefully covering your body with clothes is just foolishness.
elementary: Imagine someone who irons a perfect shirt every morning but is mean to everyone all day. Looking neat on the outside doesn’t hide the meanness. The poet says hiding your body but not fixing your faults is silly.
university: Atram (அற்றம்) here means the parts of the body to be covered, nakedness; maraiththal is covering it. Valluvar sets this against kutram (குற்றம், fault, moral defect) that remains unhidden (maraiyaa), arguing that modesty about the body while one’s faults stay on display is pullarivu, the very ‘petty understanding’ the chapter is named for. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all take ‘covering faults’ to mean removing them (neekkuthal), not concealing them, and Puliyur Kesigan adds the image of the hypocrite fully clothed and walking about ‘as though good’. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads atram differently, as ‘ruin’ or ‘loss’, giving a minority interpretation that concealing one’s downfall is the petty act. Text identical in both sources.

tamil:
அருமறை சோரும் அறிவிலான் செய்யும்
பெருமிறை தானே தனக்கு.
transliteration:
Arumarai sorum arivilaan seyyum
perumirai thaane thanakku.
current_meaning: A fool who does not keep good advice, or lets an important secret slip, does great harm to himself.
elementary: If your coach gives you a secret play and you shout it across the field, or you just forget it because you weren’t listening, your own team loses. The poet says the fool who lets good advice slip away hurts himself most.
university: The crux is arumarai sorum (அருமறை சோரும்): arumarai is ‘a rare/precious marai’, where marai may mean a secret, a hidden counsel, or a sacred teaching, and sorum means ‘lets slip, lets go loose’. Mu. Varadarasanar follows the traditional reading: the fool fails to keep a precious secret in his mind and blurts it out. Pappaiah and Kalaignar instead read it as failing to accept or follow precious advice, Puliyur Kesigan as studying the rare scriptures yet growing slack and missing their true sense, and Sivayogi Sivakumar as abandoning rare insights. All converge on the second line: perumirai (பெருமிறை, great harm or affliction) is done by the fool thaane thanakku, ‘himself to himself’, echoing 843. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
ஏவவும் செய்கலான் தான்தேறான் அவ்வுயிர்
போஒம் அளவுமோர் நோய்.
transliteration:
Evavum seygalaan thaandheraan avvuyir
poom alavumor noi.
current_meaning: A person who will not do what is right when told, and cannot figure it out alone, is like a sickness that lasts until the day they die.
elementary: Some kids can figure out on their own to pack their bag; others at least do it when Mum reminds them. But a kid who won’t think of it and won’t listen when told stays stuck forever. The poet says that kind of stubbornness is like a sickness that never goes away.
university: Valluvar names two routes to right action, being told (evavum, ஏவவும், ‘even when commanded’) and working it out oneself (thaan theral, தான் தேறல், self-ascertainment), and condemns the person who has neither. Such a life is ‘or noi’ (ஓர் நோய், a disease) until the soul departs (poom, the poetic lengthened form of pogum, marked by the alapedai -oom). Commentators differ on whose disease: Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar make it a lifelong affliction for the person himself, while Pappaiah, like the classical gloss reflected in the English ‘a burden (to the earth)’, makes him a disease to the world. Kalaignar’s idiom ‘neither sondha-puththi nor sol-puththi’ (neither one’s own wit nor heeding others’ words) neatly captures the double failure. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
காணாதான் காட்டுவான் தான்காணான் காணாதான்
கண்டானாம் தான்கண்ட வாறு.
transliteration:
Kaanaadhaan kaattuvaan thaankaanaan kaanaadhaan
kandaanaam thaankanda vaaru.
current_meaning: If you try to make a fool see the truth, you end up looking like the fool, because the fool is sure they already see everything their own way.
elementary: Try explaining to a little brother who is sure the moon follows his car that it only looks that way. He just laughs at you and says you don’t understand. The poet says that when you try to teach someone who is sure he’s right, you end up looking silly.
university: The kural is a wordplay on kaan (காண், to see): kaanaadhaan (one who does not see) is set against kaattuvaan (one who shows) and kandaan (one who has seen), and the line turns on ‘thaankanda vaaru’ (in the way he himself saw). Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as: one who tries to enlighten a fool becomes a fool himself, while the fool appears wise by his own lights; Pappaiah adds that the fool regards his teacher as the fool. Kalaignar sharpens the second half: the fool shows himself off as wise on the strength of what he alone knows. Puliyur Kesigan gives a different construal: the fool who shows others only what he saw remains one who never saw the truth. The density of the kaan-roots makes the kural famous for its sound-play. Both sources give identical text.

tamil:
உலகத்தார் உண்டென்பது இல்லென்பான் வையத்து
அலகையா வைக்கப் படும்.
transliteration:
Ulagaththaar undenbadhu illenbaan vaiyaththu
alagaiyaa vaikkap padum.
current_meaning: A person who says no to what the wise people of the world say is true will be thought of as a demon on earth.
elementary: If everyone has seen the sun rise every morning and one boy keeps insisting “There is no sun!”, people stop taking him seriously and leave him out of games. The poet says that someone who denies what everyone knows is true gets treated like a spooky outsider.
university: Ulagaththaar (உலகத்தார்) here, as often in the Kural, means not the crowd but the learned of the world (Pappaiah: ‘the great ones’, uyarndhor), and their ‘undu’ (it exists) is denied by the fool’s ‘il’ (it does not). The traditional commentators gloss what is denied as established truths such as the other world, merit and the divine, attested by the learned; Kalaignar gives a modern secular reading: denying what has been clearly shown with evidence. Such a person is placed (vaikkappadum) as an alagai (அலகை, a demon, ghost or pey) on earth, that is, shunned as something not quite human. Sivayogi Sivakumar and Mu. Varadarasanar both stress exclusion (oduhukkappaduvaan, vilakkappaduvaan). The chapter thus ends with perverse denial as the extreme of pullarivu. Text identical in both sources.

tamil:
இகலென்ப எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் பகலென்னும்
பண்பின்மை பாரிக்கும் நோய்.
transliteration:
Ikalenba ellaa uyirkkum pakalennum
panbinmai paarikkum noi.
current_meaning: Wise people call hatred a disease. In every living being, it grows the ugly habit of not getting along with others.
elementary: Think of a bad cold that spreads from one kid in class to everyone. Grudges work the same way: one person stops getting along with another, and soon nobody can play together. The poet says that kind of falling-out is a sickness, and it can catch anyone.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition: ikal (இகல், hostility, mental antagonism) is a noi (நோய், disease) that ‘spreads out’ or ‘nourishes’ (paarikkum, பாரிக்கும்) pakal (பகல், separation, non-union) in all creatures. The wordplay is deliberate: pakal normally means ‘daytime’ but here carries its older sense of ‘division’, which Puliyur Kesigan glosses as kūdāmai (கூடாமை, not coming together) and Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘failing to harmonise with other lives’. The traditional commentators following Parimelazhagar treat ikal as the inner root from which outward enmity (pagai, the subject of the next chapter, Pagaimaatchi) grows, which explains why this chapter sits in the Natpiyal (friendship) section of Porutpal. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads ikal unusually as ‘contempt’ (இகழ்ச்சி) that resists another’s nature; Kalaignar emphasises its social result, people unable to live together. The couplet text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பகல்கருதிப் பற்றா செயினும் இகல்கருதி
இன்னாசெய் யாமை தலை.
transliteration:
Pakalkarudhip patraa seyinum ikalkarudhi
innaasey yaamai thalai.
current_meaning: Even if someone who wants to fight with you does things that hurt you, the best thing is not to hurt them back out of hatred.
elementary: Suppose a classmate stops being your friend and does mean little things to you. You could plan to get back at them, but the poet says the best thing is not to. Not paying back meanness with meanness is what a really strong person does.
university: The couplet is built on a symmetry of motives: the other person acts pakal karudhi (பகல் கருதி, intending separation) and does patraa (பற்றா, unloving or disagreeable things), while you are warned against acting ikal karudhi (இகல் கருதி, out of hostility) and doing innaa (இன்னா, harmful things). The final word thalai (தலை, ‘head’, foremost) marks this restraint as the supreme course. Puliyur Kesigan and Mu. Varadarasanar both read it as forbearance under provocation; Solomon Pappaiah calls it a ‘superior quality’ (சிறந்த குணம்). The thought echoes the Aram chapters on Innaa Seyyaamai (ch. 32), especially Kural 314, but here it is set in Porutpal as practical statecraft: retaliation turns disagreement into lasting enmity. Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
இகலென்னும் எவ்வநோய் நீக்கின் தவலில்லாத்
தாவில் விளக்கம் தரும்.
transliteration:
Ikalennum evvanoi neekkin thavalillaath
thaavil vilakkam tharum.
current_meaning: If you get rid of the painful disease called hatred, you will win fame that never fades.
elementary: Imagine carrying a heavy, smelly bag of grudges everywhere you go. When you finally drop it, you feel lighter, and people start to remember you as the kind one. The poet says letting go of hostility makes you shine in a way that lasts.
university: Evvanoi (எவ்வநோய்) is a compound of evvam (எவ்வம், distress, affliction) and noi (disease): hostility is a sickness that torments its host. Its removal yields vilakkam (விளக்கம், literally ‘light, clarity’, here ‘renown, distinction’) qualified twice: thaval illaa (தவல் இல்லா, undiminishing) and thaavil (தாவில், flawless or unfailing). Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read the outcome as imperishable fame (அழியாத புகழ்), Kalaignar as ‘stainless, lasting fame’, while Sivayogi Sivakumar takes vilakkam more literally as inner clarity. The image of illness and cure continues from 851, so the chapter treats hostility medically: diagnosis (851), restraint (852), cure and its fruit (853). Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் பயக்கும் இகலென்னும்
துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்.
transliteration:
Inbaththul inbam payakkum ikalennum
thunbaththul thunbang kedin.
current_meaning: When hatred, the worst of all pains, is gone, it gives the greatest of all joys.
elementary: Have you ever made up with a friend after a big fight? That warm, happy feeling afterwards is one of the best feelings there is. The poet says being angry at someone is the worst kind of unhappy, so ending it brings the best kind of happy.
university: The couplet is a chiasmus of superlatives: inbaththul inbam (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம், joy among joys) answers thunbaththul thunbam (துன்பத்துள் துன்பம், sorrow among sorrows). The verb payakkum (பயக்கும், yields, produces) makes joy the direct fruit of hostility’s destruction (kedin, கெடின், ‘if it perishes’). Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it straightforwardly as ‘the greatest misery gone, the greatest delight comes’. The same formula ‘துன்பத்துள் துன்பம் கெடின்’ appears in Kural 369 on desire (avaa), so Valluvar ranks hostility alongside craving as the chief sources of suffering. Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
இகலெதிர் சாய்ந்தொழுக வல்லாரை யாரே
மிக்லூக்கும் தன்மை யவர்.
transliteration:
Ikaledhir saaindhozhuka vallaarai yaare
mikalookkum thanmai yavar.
current_meaning: Who could ever beat people who can turn away from hatred whenever it rises inside them?
elementary: Picture someone trying to start a fight with a kid who just smiles and won’t fight back. After a while, there is nothing to fight about, and the bully gives up. The poet says nobody can beat a person who never lets anger take over.
university: The key phrase is ikal edhir saaindhu ozhuga (இகல் எதிர் சாய்ந்து ஒழுக): to ‘lean away against’ hostility, i.e. to recoil from it and conduct oneself in the opposite direction when it arises within. Puliyur Kesigan specifies ‘when hostility arises in one’s own heart’, so the victory is first over oneself; mikal ūkkum (to aspire to overcome) then describes would-be conquerors, of whom ‘who’ (yaare) implies none. Textual note: both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print the second line as ‘மிக்லூக்கும்’ while their own romanizations read ‘mikalookkum’ and thirukkural.net’s song version prints ‘மிகலூக்கும்’; the word is mikal + ūkkum, and the printed form appears to be a shared digital orthographic slip. The same form recurs in 858. The text is otherwise identical in both sources.

tamil:
இகலின் மிகலினிது என்பவன் வாழ்க்கை
தவலும் கெடலும் நணித்து.
transliteration:
Ikalin mikalinidhu enbavan vaazhkkai
thavalum kedalum naniththu.
current_meaning: A person who thinks it is sweet to get ahead by fighting with others will soon see their life fail and fall apart.
elementary: Some people enjoy picking fights because winning feels good. But someone who always looks for a fight soon has no friends and lots of enemies, and things start to go wrong fast. The poet warns that loving fights leads to falling down.
university: Ikalin mikal inidhu (இகலின் மிகல் இனிது): ‘to excel (mikal) by means of hostility is sweet’ is the boast of the quarrelsome man. Valluvar answers that for him thavalum (தவலும், failing, slipping) and kedalum (கெடலும், perishing) are naniththu (நணித்து, near). Puliyur Kesigan reads mikal as ‘exceeding others in hostility’, Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘victory through hostility’, and Kalaignar as ‘thinking victory easy through opposition’. Pappaiah gives a distinctive reading: such a life’s survival is brief, and its ruin also comes within a brief time. The couplet turns from the inner disease to its social consequence. Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
மிகல்மேவல் மெய்ப்பொருள் காணார் இகல்மேவல்
இன்னா அறிவி னவர்.
transliteration:
Mikalmeval meypporul kaanaar ikalmeval
innaa arivi navar.
current_meaning: People whose harmful minds are set on fighting can never see the true way that leads to success.
elementary: When you are really angry at someone, it is hard to think clearly, a bit like trying to read with foggy glasses. The poet says people who love fighting have foggy minds, so they miss the smart, true way to win.
university: The couplet balances two uses of mēval (மேவல், attaching to, desiring): ikal mēval (attachment to hostility) and mikal mēval (attaining victory). Those with innaa arivu (இன்னா அறிவு, a harmful or grievous intellect) who cling to hostility cannot see meypporul (மெய்ப்பொருள், the true substance or principle) of success. Puliyur Kesigan and Solomon Pappaiah identify this ‘true substance’ with nīti nūl porul, the teaching of the treatises on statecraft, so hostility blinds a ruler to sound policy; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it more generally as ‘the truth that leads to victory’. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead splits the couplet into two statements about pride and hostility. Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
இகலிற்கு எதிர்சாய்தல் ஆக்கம் அதனை
மிக்லூக்கின் ஊக்குமாம் கேடு.
transliteration:
Ikalirku edhirsaaidhal aakkam adhanai
mikalookkin ookkumaam kedu.
current_meaning: Turning away from hatred brings good things. If you keep adding to it, harm comes rushing toward you.
elementary: A small fire can be stamped out, but if you keep feeding it sticks it grows until it burns the house. The poet says anger is like that: put it out and good things grow, feed it and trouble comes running.
university: The first line repeats the key verb of 855, edhir saaidhal (எதிர் சாய்தல், to lean away from), now naming its reward: aakkam (ஆக்கம், prosperity, growth). The second line plays on ūkkam (ஊக்கம், urging, zeal): if one urges hostility on (mikal ūkkin), ruin ‘urges itself’ (ūkkumaam kēdu) toward that person, an elegant mirroring. Puliyur Kesigan reads the first line as checking hostility before it rises in one’s own heart; Pappaiah as ‘not welcoming’ it; Kalaignar as confronting and removing it. Textual note: as in 855, both base sources print ‘மிக்லூக்கின்’ while ytamizh romanizes ‘miklookkin’; the morphology is mikal + ūkkin, and the printed cluster looks like a shared digital slip. Otherwise identical.

tamil:
இகல்காணான் ஆக்கம் வருங்கால் அதனை
மிகல்காணும் கேடு தரற்கு.
transliteration:
Ikalkaanaan aakkam varungaal adhanai
mikalkaanum kedu thararku.
current_meaning: When good times are coming, a person does not even look at hatred. When harm is coming to them, they try to make their hatred bigger.
elementary: When you are having a great day, a small bump does not bother you. But on a bad day, you might turn a tiny bump into a huge fight that makes everything worse. The poet says growing a quarrel is a sign that trouble is on its way.
university: The couplet reads hostility as a symptom of one’s turning fortune. Ikal kaanaan (இகல் காணான், ‘does not regard hostility’) when aakkam (prosperity) is coming; but to bring on kēdu (கேடு, ruin) he mikal kaanum (மிகல் காணும், ‘sees its increase’, magnifies it). Puliyur Kesigan and Pappaiah add that the fortunate man ignores hostility even with cause, while the one heading for ruin seeks it even without cause. Mu. Varadarasanar reads mikal as ‘seeking to win against it’. The underlying idea, that a mind inclines toward quarrel when its own fall is approaching, resembles the Sanskrit maxim vināśa-kāle viparīta-buddhi (‘at the time of ruin the mind turns perverse’), though Valluvar states it without fatalism. Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
இகலானாம் இன்னாத எல்லாம் நகலானாம்
நன்னயம் என்னும் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Ikalaanaam innaadha ellaam nakalaanaam
nannayam ennum serukku.
current_meaning: All painful things come from hatred. Friendliness brings the great treasure of true goodness.
elementary: Grumpy, fighting groups have lots of problems, while friendly groups share, help, and feel proud of each other. The poet ends the chapter simply: fighting brings every kind of trouble, and friendship brings goodness you can be proud of.
university: The closing couplet sets ikal against nakal (நகல், literally ‘laughing together’, hence friendship, cordiality). From ikal come innaadha ellaam (இன்னாத எல்லாம், all that is painful); from nakal comes nannayam ennum serukku (நன்னயம் என்னும் செருக்கு), ‘the elation called great good’. Puliyur Kesigan and Mu. Varadarasanar gloss nannayam as nalla nīti (good justice or policy) and serukku as perumidha nilai (a state of dignified pride); Pappaiah renders it ‘the wealth-pride of justice’, while Kalaignar reads it as ‘great joy’. Serukku usually means arrogance in the Kural, so its positive use here is notable: the only pride worth having is the dignity friendship confers. Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக ஓம்பா
மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை.
transliteration:
Valiyaarkku maaretral ombuka ombaa
meliyaarmel meka pakai.
current_meaning: Do not pick fights with people stronger than you. But do not be slow to stand against people who are weaker.
elementary: Imagine a small boat and a giant ship. A smart small boat does not try to bump the giant ship, because it would sink. Valluvar says: pick your contests wisely, and never start a fight you cannot possibly win.
university: The chapter title pakai maatchi (பகை மாட்சி) means the ‘excellence’ or right conduct of enmity: not whether a ruler will have enemies, but which enmities are worth having.
