The couplet turns on a deliberate wordplay between ombuka (ஓம்புக, ‘guard against, avoid’) and ombaa (ஓம்பா, ‘without avoiding’), and on meka (மேக, from mevu, ‘desire, take up’). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read it as plain statecraft: avoid opposing the stronger, and willingly take up enmity against the weaker; Solomon Pappaiah sharpens it to ‘if weaker, attack at once’. Mu. Karunanidhi (Kalaignar) notably inverts the moral, praising the one who spares the weak and fights the strong as the true glory of enmity, a modern ethical rereading rather than the traditional gloss. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அன்பிலன் ஆன்ற துணையிலன் தான்துவ்வான்
என்பரியும் ஏதிலான் துப்பு.
transliteration:
Anbilan aandra thunaiyilan thaanthuvvaan
enpariyum edhilaan thuppu.
current_meaning: A person who has no love for their own people, no strong friends to help, and no strength of their own, how could they ever beat a strong enemy?
elementary: Think of a team captain who is mean to his teammates, has no friends on other teams to help, and is not a strong player himself. When a tough team shows up, how can he possibly win? Kindness, friends and your own strength are what keep you safe.
university: The couplet lists three deficits: anbilan (அன்பிலன், without love, which Pappaiah and Varadarasanar read as lacking affection for kin and subjects), aandra thunaiyilan (ஆன்ற துணையிலன், without worthy or powerful allies) and thaan thuvvaan (தான் துவ்வான், himself lacking strength). The closing phrase enpariyum edhilaan thuppu (என் பரியும் ஏதிலான் துப்பு) asks how such a man could destroy (pari) the strength (thuppu) of a stranger-foe (edhilaan). Parimelazhagar reads the verse as the converse of 861: such a person is himself the ‘weak’ party whom others may safely oppose. The trio of affection, alliance and own strength mirrors the Arthashastra’s concern with internal loyalty and allies (mitra) as elements of royal power. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அஞ்சும் அறியான் அமைவிலன் ஈகலான்
தஞ்சம் எளியன் பகைக்கு.
transliteration:
Anjum ariyaan amaivilan eekalaan
thanjam eliyan pakaikku.
current_meaning: A person who is fearful, does not know what they should know, cannot get along with others, and will not share is very easy for enemies to beat.
elementary: Picture a kid who is scared of everything, doesn’t learn the rules of the game, won’t cooperate with anyone, and never shares. When trouble comes, nobody stands with him and he doesn’t know what to do. Being brave, learning, getting along and sharing are what make you strong.
university: Four faults are stacked in quick succession: anjum (அஞ்சும், he who fears, which Pappaiah glosses as fearing what need not be feared), ariyaan (அறியான், one who does not know what should be known), amaivilan (அமைவிலன், lacking accord or adaptability with others) and eekalaan (ஈகலான், one who does not give). Thanjam (தஞ்சம்) is read by the commentators as an intensifier, ‘very easily’ (Varadarasanar: மிக எளியவன்). Parimelazhagar’s logic is cumulative: fear loses battles, ignorance loses policy, unsociability loses allies and stinginess loses the army, so the foe has little left to overcome. Kalaignar renders amaivilan as lacking the habit of living in harmony and eekalaan as lacking compassion. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நீங்கான் வெகுளி நிறையிலன் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
யாங்கணும் யார்க்கும் எளிது.
transliteration:
Neengaan vekuli niraiyilan enjnaandrum
yaanganum yaarkkum elidhu.
current_meaning: A person whose anger never goes away and who cannot control themselves is easy for anyone to beat, at any time and in any place.
elementary: If a player gets angry every time and can’t keep the team’s plan a secret, the other team just has to tease him and listen in. He makes himself easy to beat. Staying calm and keeping your plans to yourself is a kind of armour.
university: Neengaan vekuli (நீங்கான் வெகுளி) is anger that does not depart, a settled irascibility rather than a passing flare. Nirai (நிறை) is the key term: Varadarasanar glosses it as the capacity to hold and govern one’s own mind, while Parimelazhagar’s tradition, followed by Solomon Pappaiah and the classic English rendering (‘neither refrains from anger nor keeps his secrets’), reads it as guarding secrets. Both senses describe a leak in self-command through which the enemy can enter. The triple universal of the second line, enjnaandrum yaanganum yaarkkum (எஞ்ஞான்றும் யாங்கணும் யார்க்கும், at all times, in all places, to all), makes the vulnerability total. This anticipates chapter 31 (vekulaamai, avoiding anger), here recast as political danger. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வழிநோக்கான் வாய்ப்பன செய்யான் பழிநோக்கான்
பண்பிலன் பற்றார்க்கு இனிது.
transliteration:
Vazhinokkaan vaayppana seyyaan pazhinokkaan
panbilan patraarkku inidhu.
current_meaning: A person who does not look for the right way, does not do what is fitting, does not care about shame, and has no good character is a joy to their enemies.
elementary: A kid who never reads the rules, doesn’t do his homework, doesn’t care if people think badly of him and isn’t kind is very easy for a rival to beat. His rival is actually happy to face him! Learning the right way and caring about your good name make you hard to beat.
university: Vazhi nokkaan (வழிநோக்கான்) is glossed by Parimelazhagar’s tradition, and by Puliyur Kesigan and Pappaiah, as one who does not study the treatises of right conduct (neethi nool); Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it more broadly as not seeking the good path. Vaayppana seyyaan (வாய்ப்பன செய்யான்) is one who fails to do what those texts enjoin or what is fitting; pazhi nokkaan (பழிநோக்கான்) disregards blame or disgrace; panbilan (பண்பிலன்) lacks character. Patraar (பற்றார்) are ‘those who do not hold to him’, that is, enemies, and inidhu (இனிது, sweet) is deliberately ironic: such a man is a pleasure to fight. The sequence moves from knowledge to action to reputation to character. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
காணாச் சினத்தான் கழிபெருங் காமத்தான்
பேணாமை பேணப் படும்.
transliteration:
Kaanaach chinaththaan kazhiperung kaamaththaan
penaamai penap padum.
current_meaning: A person who is blinded by anger and full of endless desire is a good enemy to have, because they will bring themselves down.
elementary: Imagine a rival who gets so angry he can’t see straight and wants everything he sees, right now. He runs around grabbing and shouting and forgets to defend himself. Having a rival like that is almost lucky, because his own temper and greed trip him up.
university: Kaanaach chinam (காணாச் சினம்) is anger that does not see, which Puliyur Kesigan explains as anger that blinds one to oneself and to others, and Varadarasanar as anger that does not see the truth. Kazhi perung kaamam (கழிபெருங் காமம்) is desire grown beyond all measure; Pappaiah specifies it as lust for women, while Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep the broader sense of greed or great desire. The second line plays on the root penu (to cherish): penaamai (பேணாமை, non-cherishing, i.e. enmity) penap padum (பேணப் படும், will be cherished), so his hostility is ‘to be prized’ by others. The pairing of krodha and kama as twin enemies of self-government is common to classical Indian thought. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் மன்ற அடுத்திருந்து
மாணாத செய்வான் பகை.
transliteration:
Koduththum kolalvendum mandra aduththirundhu
maanaadha seyvaan pakai.
current_meaning: If someone stays close to you but does bad things, you should certainly make them your enemy, even if it costs you something.
elementary: Suppose someone on your own team keeps quietly messing up every play. It would honestly be better if he went over to the other team, even if you had to give up something to make that happen. A clear opponent is safer than a teammate who harms you from inside.
university: The commentators divide on aduththirundhu (அடுத்திருந்து). Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as ‘staying close by’: one who remains near you as an associate yet does unworthy things (maanaadha, மாணாத) should be turned into an open enemy, even at the cost of wealth. The older line represented by Parimelazhagar, followed by Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesigan and by the classic English version (‘having begun a work, does what is not conducive’), reads it as ‘having undertaken’ an action: the enmity of a foe who mismanages his own undertakings is so advantageous that it is worth buying. Mandra (மன்ற) means ‘certainly’. Either way the paradox is that some enmity is a gain worth paying for. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
குணனிலனாய்க் குற்றம் பலவாயின் மாற்றார்க்கு
இனனிலனாம் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
transliteration:
Gunanilanaayk kutram palavaayin maatraarkku
inanilanaam emaap pudaiththu.
current_meaning: A person with no good qualities and many faults ends up with no friends to help, and that makes it easy for enemies to win.
elementary: If someone is never kind and always does mean things, little by little all his friends leave. When a problem comes, he is alone, and that makes it easy for anyone against him. Good habits are what keep friends by your side.
university: The couplet is a causal chain: gunanilan (குணனிலன், without good qualities) plus kutram pala (குற்றம் பல, many faults) yields inanilan (இனனிலன், one without kin or allies, from inam, ‘one’s own group’), and that condition is emaappu (ஏமாப்பு, security or advantage) for the maatraar (மாற்றார், adversaries). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah both stress that it is the friendlessness itself, not any action of the foe, that becomes the enemy’s strength. Kalaignar condenses this to ‘he loses his supporters and is easily brought down’. The verse links this chapter back to the Natpiyal chapters on friendship that precede it. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
செறுவார்க்குச் சேணிகவா இன்பம் அறிவிலா
அஞ்சும் பகைவர்ப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Seruvaarkkuch chenikavaa inbam arivilaa
anjum pakaivarp perin.
current_meaning: People who fight will never be far from joy if their enemies are both foolish and scared.
elementary: If you are playing a game and your opponent doesn’t understand the rules and is scared to make any move, winning becomes easy and fun. Valluvar says a foolish, frightened enemy is really a stroke of luck for the other side.
university: Seruvaar (செறுவார்) are those who attack or contend; sen ikavaa inbam (சேண் இகவா இன்பம்) is joy that does not go far away, i.e. abiding delight. Varadarasanar keeps this sense (pleasures will not depart), while Puliyur Kesigan reads it as ‘all lofty pleasures remain with them’. The enemy’s two qualities, arivilaa (அறிவிலா, without understanding, which Pappaiah specifies as without knowledge of what is just) and anjum (அஞ்சும், fearing), recapitulate the first two faults of 863. Kalaignar renders the joy specifically as the joy of victory. The verse is the offensive counterpart to the chapter’s earlier defensive lists. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கல்லான் வெகுளும் சிறுபொருள் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
ஒல்லானை ஒல்லா தொளி.
transliteration:
Kallaan vekulum siruporul enjnaandrum
ollaanai ollaa tholi.
current_meaning: A person who will not take even the small, easy win of fighting an enemy who knows nothing will never become famous.
elementary: If you won’t even try an easy level of a game, how will you ever beat the hard ones and earn a trophy? Valluvar says that someone who shies away from small, easy challenges never earns a great name.
university: The syntax is compressed: kallaan vekulum siruporul (கல்லான் வெகுளும் சிறுபொருள்) is ‘the small gain of being angry with (fighting) the unlearned man’, and ollaanai ollaadhu oli (ஒல்லானை ஒல்லாது ஒளி) says that light, i.e. fame, will not unite with the one who does not obtain it. Varadarasanar on thirukkural.net reads: one who cannot do the easy thing of opposing the unlearned will never gain glory; Pappaiah adds that the gain from fighting one ignorant of the treatises is small, yet the king who disdains it earns no renown; Kalaignar has fame mock such a man for hesitating even before untrained foes. Note: ytamizh.com’s Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar glosses for 870 are misplaced (they discuss forgiving old friends, the theme of kural 810); the couplet text itself is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பகைஎன்னும் பண்பி லதனை ஒருவன்
நகையேயும் வேண்டற்பாற்று அன்று.
transliteration:
Pakaiennum panpi ladhanai oruvan
nakaiyeyum ventarpaatru andru.
current_meaning: Hatred has nothing good in it. No one should want it, not even as a game or a joke.
elementary: Some kids pretend to be enemies just for fun, teasing and picking fights as a joke. The poet says even pretend enmity is a bad game, because a joke fight can quickly turn into a real one that nobody can stop.
university: The chapter opens by naming its subject with a moral label: pakai (பகை, enmity) is panpiladhu (பண்பிலது), ‘that which is devoid of good quality’. The emphatic nakaiyeyum (நகையேயும், ‘even in jest / even in play’) carries the force of the couplet: enmity is not to be courted even in sport, still less in earnest. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as an evil without merit that should not be desired even as a pastime, and Kalaignar explains that enmity runs contrary to good character; Puliyur Kesigan adds that this is the settled conclusion of the ethical treatises. The placement is notable: in a chapter that goes on to give hard-headed advice about handling enemies, Valluvar first insists that enmity itself is never desirable. The text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net, which titles the chapter பகைத்திறந் தெரிதல் with a word break.

tamil:
வில்லேர் உழவர் பகைகொளினும் கொள்ளற்க
சொல்லேர் உழவர் பகை.
transliteration:
Viller uzhavar pakaikolinum kollarka
soller uzhavar pakai.
current_meaning: Even if you must make enemies of soldiers who use the bow as their plow, never make enemies of wise people who use words as their plow.
elementary: A bully with big muscles can only hurt you while he is near you. But a clever person who writes and speaks well can tell your story to the whole town and to people years from now. So the poet says: if you must quarrel with anyone, never quarrel with the people who are good with words.
university: The couplet is built on a celebrated agricultural metaphor: villēr uḻavar (வில்லேர் உழவர்) are ‘ploughmen whose plough is the bow’, that is, warriors, while collēr uḻavar (சொல்லேர் உழவர்) are ‘ploughmen whose plough is the word’. Mu. Varadarasanar reads the latter as scholars, Solomon Pappaiah as writers, Kalaignar as learned people of verbal power; the older commentarial tradition, reflected in Pope’s gloss ‘ministers whose ploughs are words’, takes them as counsellors skilled in policy. The concessive kolinum (‘even if you incur’) does not recommend war with soldiers; it ranks dangers, implying that the harm of hostile counsel, satire or reputation outlasts and outreaches the harm of arms. The metaphor also suggests that both kinds of men ‘cultivate’ a harvest, and the harvest of words is wider. No variant readings appear between ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஏமுற் றவரினும் ஏழை தமியனாய்ப்
பல்லார் பகைகொள் பவன்.
transliteration:
Emur ravarinum ezhai thamiyanaaip
pallaar pakaikol pavan.
current_meaning: A person who is alone and still makes enemies of many people is more foolish than someone who has lost their mind.
elementary: Picture one kid on the playground who has no friends on his side, yet goes around picking fights with every group. Even someone who is not thinking clearly would not do that. The poet says this is the silliest thing a person can do.
university: The comparison turns on ēmuṟṟavar (ஏமுற்றவர்), ‘those who are deluded or deranged’: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah gloss them as the mad (பித்தர்), Kalaignar as the arrogant, while Sivayogi Sivakumar reads ‘the despised’. Ēḻai (ஏழை) here means ‘senseless, witless’, not ‘poor’, as all the commentators agree. Tamiyaṉāy (‘being alone’) and pallār (‘many’) set up the arithmetic: a man without allies who collects many enemies has made the one choice even a madman might avoid. Pappaiah applies it directly to a ruler (ஆட்சியாளன்), in keeping with the Porutpal setting. The text matches in both ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பகைநட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும் பண்புடை யாளன்
தகைமைக்கண் தங்கிற்று உலகு.
transliteration:
Pakainatpaak kontozhukum panputai yaalan
thakaimaikkan thangitru ulaku.
current_meaning: The world is safe because of the greatness of a kind person who makes enemies into friends and lives that way.
elementary: Imagine a kid who gets pushed by someone, and instead of pushing back, invites that person to play and they become best friends. The poet says people like that are so great that the whole world is held together by them.
university: After three couplets warning against enmity, Valluvar names the ideal: the paṇpuṭaiyāḷaṉ (பண்புடையாளன், ‘man of noble character’) who conducts himself (oḻukum) by making pakai into naṭpu (நட்பு, friendship). Takaimai (தகைமை) is greatness or excellence, and taṅkiṟṟu ulaku (‘the world abides’) is a strong claim: the stability of the world itself depends on such people. Mu. Varadarasanar speaks of the world resting in his magnanimity; Solomon Pappaiah reads it of a ruler who converts enemies and lives with them, so that the world falls within his greatness; Kalaignar has the whole world praising such a person; Sivayogi Sivakumar says the world endures through such honoured conduct. Pope renders it as ‘worthy rule can change his foes to friends’, keeping the political frame. The couplet links back to Chapter 87 and forward to the strategic advice in 875.

tamil:
தன்துணை இன்றால் பகையிரண்டால் தான்ஒருவன்
இன்துணையாக் கொள்கவற்றின் ஒன்று.
transliteration:
Thandhunai indraal pakaiyirantaal thaanoruvan
indhunaiyaak kolkavatrin ondru.
current_meaning: If you have no one to help you and you face two enemies alone, make one of them your friend.
elementary: Suppose two bigger kids are both upset with you and nobody is on your side. Instead of fighting both, you make peace with one of them, and suddenly it is two against one in your favour. That is the smart move the poet recommends.
university: This is the most explicitly strategic couplet of the chapter. Three conditions are stacked in clipped clauses: taṉtuṇai iṉṟāl (‘if one has no support’), pakai iraṇṭāl (‘if the enemies are two’), tāṉ oruvaṉ (‘and one is alone’). The remedy is to take one of the two as iṉtuṇai (இன்துணை), a ‘sweet’ or agreeable ally. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as a general maxim, while Solomon Pappaiah again frames it for a ruler; Sivayogi Sivakumar keeps it close to the text. It complements 874: where that couplet praised turning enemies into friends as a virtue, this one treats it as a necessity of statecraft, in line with the Indian political tradition of alliances among neighbouring powers. The text is identical in both sources.

tamil:
தேறினும் தேறா விடினும் அழிவின்கண்
தேறான் பகாஅன் விடல்.
transliteration:
Therinum theraa vitinum azhivinkan
theraan pakaaan vital.
current_meaning: In a time of trouble, whether you have tested a person before or not, do not get too close to them and do not cut them off. Keep a careful distance.
elementary: When something big goes wrong, it is not the time to suddenly make a new best friend or to start a new fight. The poet says: stay polite and keep a bit of distance, and wait until things are calm before deciding who to trust.
university: This is among the most compressed and debated couplets of the chapter. The verb tēṟu (தேறு, ‘to trust, be convinced about’) appears three times: tēṟiṉum tēṟā viṭiṉum (‘whether one has trusted him or not’), then tēṟāṉ (‘not trusting’) paired with pakāaṉ (பகாஅன், ‘not separating’, with the alapedai lengthening), ending in viṭal (‘leave him so’). Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as: whether you had earlier assessed a man or not, in a time of ruin neither trust him nor drop him; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar apply it specifically to an enemy, advising neither closeness nor open rupture; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as ‘do not approach the untrustworthy in ruinous times’. Pope’s verse is loose, and his explanation ‘neither to join nor separate’ follows the traditional reading. The thirukkural.net English summary, ‘be wary of joining or opposing any’, captures the consensus: in crisis, keep a guarded neutrality. The text matches in both sources.

tamil:
நோவற்க நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு மேவற்க
மென்மை பகைவர் அகத்து.
transliteration:
Novarka nondhadhu ariyaarkku mevarka
menmai pakaivar akaththu.
current_meaning: Do not tell your troubles to people who do not already know about them, and do not show your weak points to your enemies.
elementary: If you are feeling hurt, you do not have to tell everyone you meet. And if someone is being mean to you, try not to show them where it hurts, because they might poke you there again. Share your worries with the people who really care and already understand.
university: The couplet has two prohibitions in parallel: nōvaṟka (‘do not lament’) to those who do not know one’s suffering, and mēvaṟka (‘do not take on, display’) meṉmai (மென்மை, ‘softness, weakness’) in the presence of enemies. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take the first line as referring to friends who have not themselves perceived one’s distress: to complain to them is undignified and spreads knowledge of one’s weakness. Solomon Pappaiah reads the hidden object of both lines as ‘our lack of strength’, which should neither be told to unaware friends nor shown to enemies. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the lines quite differently: do not grieve over those who do not understand grief, and do not covet the soft spot of enemies. Pope’s ‘To those who know them not, complain not of your woes; nor to your foeman’s eyes infirmities disclose’ follows the majority reading. The text is identical in both sources.

tamil:
வகையறிந்து தற்செய்து தற்காப்ப மாயும்
பகைவர்கண் பட்ட செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Vakaiyarindhu tharseydhu tharkaappa maayum
pakaivarkan patta serukku.
current_meaning: Know the right way to act, build up your strength, and protect yourself well. Then your enemies’ pride will fade away by itself.
elementary: If a team keeps teasing yours, the best answer is not to shout back but to practise, get stronger, and play smart. When they see how ready you are, their boasting stops on its own.
university: Three participial steps lead to the result: vakai aṟintu (‘knowing the method’), taṟceytu (‘making oneself strong’), taṟkāppa (‘guarding oneself’); then māyum (‘will perish’) the cerukku (செருக்கு, ‘pride, arrogance, exultation’) that has arisen in the enemies. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read cerukku as the enemy’s pride, which collapses without a blow once one is prepared; Solomon Pappaiah adds that taṟkāppa includes guarding one’s secrets, linking back to 877; Pope’s explanation renders cerukku as the foes’ ‘joy’ and taṟceytu as ‘securing assistance’, a reading that ties the couplet to 875. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as knowing one’s qualifications and self-protection. The point is deterrence: preparation defeats an enemy’s confidence before any conflict. The text matches in both sources.

tamil:
இளைதாக முள்மரம் கொல்க களையுநர்
கைகொல்லும் காழ்த்த இடத்து.
transliteration:
Ilaidhaaka mulmaram kolka kalaiyunar
kaikollum kaazhththa itaththu.
current_meaning: Cut down a thorny tree while it is still young. Once it grows hard, it will hurt the hand of the person who tries to cut it.
elementary: A tiny thorny weed in the garden can be pulled out with two fingers. If you leave it for a year, it grows big, tough thorns that scratch your hands when you finally try to pull it. Problems are the same: deal with them while they are small.
university: The couplet is a pure agricultural image applied to enmity, as all the commentators make explicit: iḷaitāka (‘while young’) muḷmaram (முள்மரம், ‘thorn tree’) kolka (‘destroy’); otherwise, kāḻtta iṭattu (‘when it has hardened’, from kāḻ, the hard heartwood) it kai kollum (‘destroys the hand’) of the kaḷaiyunar (களையுநர், ‘those who weed it out’). Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the literal image; Kalaignar draws the lesson that enmity must be put down before it matures; Sivayogi Sivakumar adds the explicit note that enmity must not be allowed to grow. Solomon Pappaiah reads the thorn tree as one who intends to destroy us. The verb kol- (‘kill’) appears in both lines, giving a pointed reversal: kill it, or it kills your hand. The text matches in both sources.

tamil:
உயிர்ப்ப உளரல்லர் மன்ற செயிர்ப்பவர்
செம்மல் சிதைக்கலா தார்.
transliteration:
Uyirppa ularallar mandra seyirppavar
semmal sidhaikkalaa thaar.
current_meaning: People who do not break the pride of enemies who hurt them are not truly alive, even though they still breathe.
elementary: If someone keeps bullying a group and nobody ever stands up to them, the bully only gets bolder. The poet says that people who never stand up to proud, hostile enemies are not really living freely at all.
university: The closing couplet is the chapter’s sharpest. Uyirppa (உயிர்ப்ப, ‘so much as to breathe’) uḷar allar (‘they do not exist’) maṉṟa (மன்ற, ‘certainly’): such people are not alive even to breathe. The condition is that they cannot citaikkal (‘shatter’) the cemmal (செம்மல், ‘pride, eminence, haughtiness’) of ceyirppavar (செயிர்ப்பவர், ‘those who are hostile or offend’). Kalaignar reads it as: those who cannot break the enemies’ arrogance cannot truly be called alive just because they breathe; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as a prediction that such people will be destroyed within a breath; Mu. Varadarasanar’s printed gloss on ytamizh reads ‘தலைமையைக் கொடுக்க’, which appears to be a typographic slip for கெடுக்க (‘destroy’). Sivayogi Sivakumar takes ceyirppavar as open wrongdoers. Read with 871 and 874, the chapter’s logic is clear: never seek enmity, convert it where possible, but where it persists, deal with it decisively. The text matches in both sources.

tamil:
நிழல்நீரும் இன்னாத இன்னா தமர்நீரும்
இன்னாவாம் இன்னா செயின்.
transliteration:
Nizhalneerum innaadha innaa thamarneerum
innaavaam innaa seyin.
current_meaning: Shade and water are pleasant, but they are bad when they make you sick. In the same way, your own relatives become painful when they do you harm.
elementary: A shady tree and a cool drink are lovely on a hot day, but if the water is dirty it can make you sick. Family and friends are meant to be like shade and water, so when someone close to us starts hurting us, it feels even worse than a stranger doing it.
university: The chapter opens with a paired simile: nizhal-neer (நிழல்நீர், shade and water), the archetypal comforts of a hot land, are innaadha (இன்னாத, painful) when innaa (இன்னா, harmful, i.e. disease-bearing); so too thamar-neer (தமர்நீர், the 'nature' or disposition of one's kin) becomes innaavaam when it does harm. The wordplay on neer, meaning both 'water' and 'nature/quality', is deliberate and is reflected in Mu. Varadarasanar's and Kalaignar's glosses, which read thamar-neer as the qualities of kinsfolk. Solomon Pappaiah extends thamar to one's own party or faction, showing how modern commentators read utpakai (உட்பகை, enmity from within) politically as well as domestically. In the traditional reading framed by Parimelazhagar, the Porul section addresses a ruler, so the 'kin' include courtiers and relations around the throne. Text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வாள்போல பகைவரை அஞ்சற்க அஞ்சுக
கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Vaalpola pakaivarai anjarka anjuka
kelpol pakaivar thotarpu.
current_meaning: Do not fear enemies who come at you openly like a drawn sword. Fear enemies who pretend to be your relatives or friends.
elementary: A bully who shouts at you from across the playground is easy to spot and avoid. The trickier problem is someone who pretends to be your friend while secretly trying to get you in trouble, so that is the person to be careful about.
university: The couplet sets two kinds of foe against each other: vaal-pola pakaivar (வாள்போல பகைவர், foes like a sword), whose hostility is open and therefore manageable, and kel-pol pakaivar (கேள்போல் பகைவர், foes who appear as kel, 'kin' or intimates). The imperative pair anjarka / anjuka (அஞ்சற்க / அஞ்சுக, 'fear not' / 'fear') gives the verse its antithetical snap. What is to be feared is their thodarpu (தொடர்பு), the ongoing association, since closeness is the very channel through which the hidden enemy works. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the second group as those who behave like relatives while harbouring utpakai, and Pope renders them 'foes who seem like kinsmen'. The text agrees in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உட்பகை அஞ்சித்தற் காக்க உலைவிடத்து
மட்பகையின் மாணத் தெறும்.
transliteration:
Utpakai anjiththar kaakka ulaivitaththu
matpakaiyin maanath therum.
current_meaning: Fear the enemy within your own circle and protect yourself. When you are weak, it will cut you down as surely as a potter’s tool cuts clay.
elementary: A potter uses a thin wire or blade to slice through soft clay in one easy stroke. Hidden enemies wait for a time when you are tired or in trouble, and then they can hurt you just as easily, so it is wise to watch out for them early.
university: The verse pairs a command, utpakai anji thar kaakka (உட்பகை அஞ்சித் தற்காக்க, 'fearing internal enmity, guard yourself'), with a warning about timing: ulaividaththu (உலைவிடத்து), 'at the time of tottering' or decline. The image matpakai (மட்பகை), literally 'clay-enemy', is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as the potter's cutting tool that slices clay vessels, so that maana therum (மாணத் தெறும்) means 'will destroy thoroughly'. Pope's 'potter's knife' follows the same reading. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads the second line as setting a cooking pot on an unfired clay vessel, an interpretive variant rather than a textual one. The Tamil text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மனமாணா உட்பகை தோன்றின் இனமாணா
ஏதம் பலவும் தரும்.
transliteration:
Manamaanaa utpakai thondrin inamaanaa
edham palavum tharum.
current_meaning: If hidden hatred grows from a mind that is not good, it brings many troubles and turns a person's own people against them.
elementary: If a person keeps a secret grudge and refuses to let it go, it slowly spoils everything around them. Soon brothers, sisters and friends are arguing and taking sides, and the whole group stops getting along.
university: The verse balances two negated compounds: mana-maanaa (மனமாணா, 'mind not made excellent', i.e. unreformed or unreconciled) and ina-maanaa (இனமாணா, 'kin not made excellent', i.e. kinsfolk who fall out of harmony). When utpakai arises in the first, it yields edham palavum (ஏதம் பலவும், many faults or evils) of the second kind. Mu. Varadarasanar reads the result as many faults that keep one's kin from being set right, while Kalaignar says such a disposition makes one's own people into enemies. Pope's 'secret enmities ... that minds pervert' and the thirukkural.net rendering 'myriad miseries manifest among kin' both preserve the link between inner hostility and outer estrangement. No textual variant is attested between ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உறல்முறையான் உட்பகை தோன்றின் இறல்முறையான்
ஏதம் பலவும் தரும்.
transliteration:
Uralmuraiyaan utpakai thondrin iralmuraiyaan
edham palavum tharum.
current_meaning: If hidden hatred grows among relatives, it brings many deadly troubles.
elementary: When a family has a big fight that nobody fixes, it can grow worse and worse until it breaks the family apart. The poet says a quarrel inside the family can be the most dangerous kind of all.
university: The couplet turns on a chiming pair: ural-muraiyaan (உறல்முறையான், 'by way of relationship') and iral-muraiyaan (இறல்முறையான், 'by way of death'). Where enmity springs from kinship, it yields evils of a deadly kind. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as 'many sufferings of the kind that kill', and Solomon Pappaiah as 'many faults joined with death'. Pope's explanation speaks of internal hatred 'in a (king's) family' leading to 'fatal crime', showing the royal framing of the traditional commentary, where kin-enmity means dynastic feud. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads iral-muraiyaan differently, as harm extending even to those outside the kin, an interpretive variant. The Tamil text agrees in both sources.

tamil:
ஒன்றாமை ஒன்றியார் கட்படின் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
பொன்றாமை ஒன்றல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Ondraamai ondriyaar katpatin egngnaandrum
pondraamai ondral aridhu.
current_meaning: Once fighting starts among people who were united, it is always hard to escape being destroyed.
elementary: Think of a team that always played together well. If the players start secretly disliking each other, they stop passing the ball and stop helping, and soon even an easy match is lost. Once a group splits, it is very hard to stop it from falling apart.
university: The couplet is a study in the root ondru (ஒன்று, 'to be one, to unite'): ondraamai (ஒன்றாமை, disunity) arises among ondriyaar (ஒன்றியார், those who were united), and then pondraamai ondral (பொன்றாமை ஒன்றல், 'attaining non-perishing', i.e. escaping ruin) becomes aridhu (அரிது, difficult) egngnaandrum (எஞ்ஞான்றும், at any time). Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as: when enmity arises among one's own people, it is always hard to avoid perishing through that internal enmity; Solomon Pappaiah applies it to a government whose fall cannot then be prevented. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as the difficulty of ever reuniting once a group is split by another's intrigue. Both sources print the same text, and thirukkural.net transliterates katpatin, reflecting the sandhi of kan + padin.

tamil:
செப்பின் புணர்ச்சிபோல் கூடினும் கூடாதே
உட்பகை உற்ற குடி.
transliteration:
Seppin punarchchipol kootinum kootaadhe
utpakai utra kuti.
current_meaning: A family full of hidden hatred may look joined together like a box and its lid, but it is never truly united.
elementary: A box and its lid fit together neatly, but they are still two separate pieces that can be pulled apart at any moment. A family that is secretly angry inside may look together at dinner, but deep down they are not really united.
university: The governing image is seppin punarchchi (செப்பின் புணர்ச்சி, 'the joining of a seppu'), a small casket whose lid sits flush on its body so that the two look like one object. A kudi (குடி, family, clan or community) that has suffered utpakai may koodinum (கூடினும், even though it comes together) yet kootaadhu (கூடாதே, will surely not unite). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read seppu as a lidded casket, and Pope translates 'casket with its cover'. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads seppu as copper used to join two different metals, an interpretive variant. Pappaiah extends kudi to the party and the state. The text is identical in both sources.

tamil:
அரம்பொருத பொன்போலத் தேயும் உரம்பொருது
உட்பகை உற்ற குடி.
transliteration:
Aramporudha ponpolath theyum uramporudhu
utpakai utra kuti.
current_meaning: A family with hatred inside wears itself down and loses its strength, like metal worn away by a file.
elementary: When you rub a file back and forth on a piece of metal, a little dust falls off each time until the metal gets thinner and thinner. A family that keeps fighting inside loses a little strength every day in the same way, until there is not much left.
university: The image is aram porudha pon (அரம் பொருத பொன், metal struck by a file), which theyum (தேயும், wears away). The second line, uram porudhu (உரம் பொருது), means that the family's own strength (uram) is ground away by the friction of utpakai. Pon usually means gold, as Pope and thirukkural.net render it, but Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss it as iron (இரும்பு), reflecting the wider sense of pon as metal. The echo of porudha / porudhu (struck / striking) emphasises that the family is both the file and the metal, wearing itself down. The text agrees in both sources.

tamil:
எட்பக வன்ன சிறுமைத்தே ஆயினும்
உட்பகை உள்ளதாங் கேடு.
transliteration:
Etpaka vanna sirumaiththe aayinum
utpakai ulladhaang ketu.
current_meaning: Even if hatred inside a group is as small as half a sesame seed, ruin is hiding inside it.
elementary: A sesame seed is one of the tiniest seeds there is, and half a seed is smaller still. The poet says even a grudge that small, kept hidden inside a group, can grow until it breaks everything apart.
university: The measure of smallness is etpakavu (எட்பகவு, the split half of a sesame seed), among the tiniest units in Tamil idiom; anna (அன்ன) means 'like'. However sirumaiththu (சிறுமைத்து, slight) the utpakai is, ketu (கேடு, ruin) is ulladhu (உள்ளது, present) within it. Mu. Varadarasanar says that even at that size it carries ruin able to destroy a whole family, and Solomon Pappaiah reads it as destruction already present inside the faction. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads 'ulladhu' as 'all that exists', giving 'ruin to everything', a reading the word order allows. The thirukkural.net rendering ('even a dissent as small as a seed') and Pope ('slight as shred of sesame seed') agree with the dominant reading. The text is identical in both sources.

tamil:
உடம்பாடு இலாதவர் வாழ்க்கை குடங்கருள்
பாம்போடு உடனுறைந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Utampaatu ilaadhavar vaazhkkai kutangarul
paampotu utanurain thatru.
current_meaning: Living with people who do not truly agree with you is like sharing a small hut with a snake.
elementary: Imagine sleeping in a tiny tent with a snake curled up in the corner. You could never relax, because you would always be wondering when it might bite. Living with someone who secretly dislikes you feels the same way.
university: The closing couplet gives the chapter its most vivid image. Utampaatu ilaadhavar (உடம்பாடு இலாதவர்) are 'those without inner agreement', people who share one's life without sharing one's mind. To live with them is kutangarul paampotu utanurainthatru (குடங்கருள் பாம்போடு உடனுறைந்தற்று), 'like dwelling together with a snake inside a kutangar'. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah gloss kutangar as a small hut (குடிசை), and Kalaignar stresses the moment-by-moment fear of such a life. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as a dark cave, an interpretive variant. Pope's 'dwelling in a shed with snake for company' and thirukkural.net's 'share a hut with a cobra' agree on the hut reading. The text is identical in both sources.

tamil:
ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் இகழாமை போற்றுவார்
போற்றலுள் எல்லாம் தலை.
transliteration:
Aatruvaar aatral ikazhaamai potruvaar
potraluL ellaam thalai.
current_meaning: Of all the ways a careful person can protect themselves, the first is never to look down on people who have the power to do whatever they set out to do.
elementary: Imagine a small puppy barking and nipping at a big, calm elephant. The safest thing the puppy can do is simply not tease the elephant. Being respectful to people who are strong and capable is the best way to keep yourself out of trouble.
university: The opening couplet frames the whole adhikaram as a matter of self-protection: poatruvaar (போற்றுவார், those who guard themselves) have many kinds of poatral (போற்றல், guarding, watchfulness), but the thalai (தலை, head, foremost) of them all is ikazhaamai (இகழாமை, not despising) the aatral (ஆற்றல், power, capability) of aatruvaar (ஆற்றுவார், those able to carry out what they undertake). Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary associated with Parimelazhagar, reads the chapter in the setting of statecraft: having discussed internal enmity (Ch. 89), Valluvar now warns the king and his men against offending two classes of the great, the mighty in worldly power and the great in spiritual power (ascetics). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both gloss aatruvaar as one able to complete a chosen task, while Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as those who lead and guide. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பெரியாரைப் பேணாது ஒழுகிற் பெரியாரால்
பேரா இடும்பை தரும்.
transliteration:
Periyaaraip penaadhu ozhukir periyaaraal
peraa itumpai tharum.
current_meaning: If you act without respect for great people, they will bring you trouble that never goes away.
elementary: If you keep ignoring your coach and being rude, you might find yourself benched for the whole season. Not treating important people with respect can bring trouble that doesn’t go away quickly.
university: The couplet turns on the repeated periyaar (பெரியார், the great): conduct (ozhugal, ஒழுகல்) that does not penu (பேணு, cherish, honour) the great yields, through those same great ones, peraa idumbai (பேரா இடும்பை, affliction that does not depart). The adjective peraa (from pe-, to move away) stresses permanence, which Mu. Varadarasanar renders as நீங்காத துன்பம். Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it simply as disrespect to elders or great persons, while the traditional reading behind Pope’s explanation glosses periyaar as powerful rulers. The phrase periyaaraal (by the great) shows that the harm is not mere fate but the active response of the offended party. Both sources agree on the text, including the sandhi form ஒழுகிற்.

tamil:
கெடல்வேண்டின் கேளாது செய்க அடல்வேண்டின்
ஆற்று பவர்கண் இழுக்கு.
transliteration:
Ketalventin kelaadhu seyka atalventin
aatru pavarkan izhukku.
current_meaning: If you want to ruin yourself, act without listening to advice. If you want to be destroyed, do wrong to people who have great power.
elementary: If you poke a sleeping bear with a stick and ignore everyone shouting stop, you are asking for trouble. Valluvar says, with a wink: if you want to get hurt, go ahead and annoy the strongest one around.
university: This couplet uses irony: keDal veNDin (கெடல் வேண்டின், if you desire ruin), keLaadhu seyga (கேளாது செய்க, do it without listening), izhukku (இழுக்கு, offence, fault) toward aatrupavar (ஆற்றுபவர், those able) aDal veNDin (அடல் வேண்டின், when they wish to slay). The phrase keLaadhu is read differently: Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary, takes it as not listening to the righteous dictates of law or the nīti texts, and Solomon Pappaiah likewise speaks of ignoring what the moral treatises say; Kalaignar reads it as not listening to anyone’s advice; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the first half more freely as a separate clause. The pairing keDal/aDal is a typical Valluvar sound-echo. The text is identical in both sources, which print ஆற்று பவர்கண் with the metrical split.

tamil:
கூற்றத்தைக் கையால் விளித்தற்றால் ஆற்றுவார்க்கு
ஆற்றாதார் இன்னா செயல்.
transliteration:
Kootraththaik kaiyaal viliththatraal aatruvaarkku
aatraadhaar innaa seyal.
current_meaning: When weak people harm strong people, it is like waving to Death with their own hand to come and take them.
elementary: A tiny mouse that pulls a lion’s tail is basically waving and calling, Come and get me! When someone weak picks a fight with someone much stronger, they are inviting their own trouble.
university: The image is vivid: kootram (கூற்றம், Death, Yama, the god who divides life from body) is summoned kaiyaal viLiththu (கையால் விளித்து, by beckoning with the hand). The comparison applies to aatraadhaar (ஆற்றாதார், those without power) doing innaa (இன்னா, harm) to aatruvaar (ஆற்றுவார், the powerful). Solomon Pappaiah specifies the three kinds of power, of wisdom, wealth and army, and adds that it is the weak who strike first; Mu. Varadarasanar stresses that Yama would come of himself anyway, so the weak only hasten it. The couplet carries forward kural 891’s key word aatruvaar, binding the chapter together. Text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
யாண்டுச்சென்று யாண்டும் உளராகார் வெந்துப்பின்
வேந்து செறப்பட் டவர்.
transliteration:
Yaantuchchendru yaantum ularaakaar vendhuppin
vendhu serappat tavar.
current_meaning: People who make a fierce and powerful king angry will not survive, wherever they run to.
elementary: Playing hide-and-seek with someone who can see everywhere is no fun, because there is nowhere to hide. If you make a very powerful ruler angry, no hiding place is safe.
university: Here the great one is a vendhu (வேந்து, king) of vem-thuppu (வெந்துப்பு, fierce strength); those seRappaTTavar (செறப்பட்டவர், who have incurred his wrath, from seRu, to be angry) will be uLar aakaar (உளர் ஆகார், will not exist, will not live) yaaNDu senRu yaaNDum (wherever they go, anywhere). Solomon Pappaiah and Mu. Varadarasanar agree that the offender cannot live anywhere; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads uLar aakaar more psychologically, as being unable to settle. Pope’s rendering notes they will not prosper wherever they go. The two sources agree on the text; thirukkural.net’s transliteration shows the metrical division வெந்துப்பின் / வேந்து, with the split செறப்பட் டவர் in both.

tamil:
எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம் உய்யார்
பெரியார்ப் பிழைத்தொழுகு வார்.
transliteration:
Eriyaal sutappatinum uyvuntaam uyyaar
periyaarp pizhaiththozhuku vaar.
current_meaning: A person caught in a fire may still survive, but people who keep doing wrong to the great will not escape.
elementary: Getting burnt by a campfire hurts, but you can heal. Valluvar says that hurting truly great people is even more dangerous than fire, because there may be no getting better from it.
university: The comparison is a fortiori: eri (எரி, fire) can burn a man and still uyvu uNDaam (உய்வு உண்டாம், there may be escape, survival), but uyyaar (உய்யார், they will not survive) who periyaarp pizhaiththu ozhuguvaar (பெரியார்ப் பிழைத்து ஒழுகுவார், live in offence against the great). The chapter title itself comes from this root, pizhai (பிழை, fault, offence). Pope’s explanation, reflecting the traditional commentary, glosses the fire as a forest fire and the great as devotees or ascetics, whose spiritual power is pictured as more consuming than physical flame. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the great as those of surpassing power generally. The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
வகைமாண்ட வாழ்க்கையும் வான்பொருளும் என்னாம்
தகைமாண்ட தக்கார் செறின்.
transliteration:
Vakaimaanta vaazhkkaiyum vaanporulum ennaam
thakaimaanta thakkaar serin.
current_meaning: If truly great people with fine character become angry with someone, what good are that person’s grand life and great riches?
elementary: You could have the biggest toy collection in the world, but if you are mean to the kindest, wisest grown-up in town, everyone will stop trusting you. All your toys can’t fix that. Good people’s goodwill is worth more than riches.
university: Two pairs balance each other: vagai maaNDa vaazhkkai (வகைமாண்ட வாழ்க்கை, a life excellent in every kind) and vaan poruL (வான்பொருள், sky-high wealth) are worth ennaam (என்னாம், what will they become?) if thagai maaNDa thakkaar (தகைமாண்ட தக்கார், the worthy, distinguished in noble quality) seRin (செறின், are angered). Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary, applies this to a king whose government with all its auxiliaries and untold wealth is useless before the wrath of the righteous great; Solomon Pappaiah glosses the great as those excellent in character. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the couplet differently, as saying that wealth and splendour cannot equal the richness of the worthy, showing an alternative interpretation of seRin. Both sources print the same text.

tamil:
குன்றன்னார் குன்ற மதிப்பின் குடியொடு
நின்றன்னார் மாய்வர் நிலத்து.
transliteration:
Kundrannaar kundra madhippin kutiyotu
nindrannaar maaivar nilaththu.
current_meaning: If great people, firm as mountains, are looked down on, even those who seemed firmly settled on earth will be wiped out along with their families.
elementary: Think of a mountain: it is big, steady and old. If you try to knock a mountain down, you will only hurt yourself. People who are great like mountains deserve respect, and those who treat them badly can lose everything, even their family’s good name.
university: The couplet plays on kunRu (குன்று, hill, mountain) and kunRa (குன்ற, to diminish): if kunRannaar (குன்றன்னார், those like mountains) are kunRa madhikkap paDin (thought of as diminished, slighted), or, in another reading, if they madhi (மதி, resolve) on diminishing someone, then even ninRannaar (நின்றன்னார், those who seem to stand forever) maaivar (மாய்வர், will perish) kuDiyoDu (குடியொடு, along with their lineage) nilaththu (நிலத்து, on earth). The two readings are visible in the commentaries: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as the mountain-like great resolving on destruction, while Sivayogi Sivakumar and Kalaignar take it as others belittling the great. Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary, identifies the mountain-like ones as devotees. The text is identical in both sources.

tamil:
ஏந்திய கொள்கையார் சீறின் இடைமுரிந்து
வேந்தனும் வேந்து கெடும்.
transliteration:
Endhiya kolkaiyaar seerin itaimurindhu
vendhanum vendhu ketum.
current_meaning: When people with high ideals rise up in anger, even a king will be broken in the middle of his rule and lose his kingdom.
elementary: Imagine a team captain who bullies the fairest, most honest player. When the whole team sees it and stands with that honest player, the captain loses the job. Even powerful people can fall if they anger those who live by high principles.
university: Eendhiya koLgaiyaar (ஏந்திய கொள்கையார்) are those who bear aloft high principles or vows; if they seeRin (சீறின், flare up in anger), even the vendhan (வேந்தன், king) will iDai murindhu (இடை முரிந்து, be broken midway) and vendhu keDum (வேந்து கெடும், his kingship will perish). Pope’s explanation glosses the king as Indra and the great as those of exalted vows, reflecting the traditional commentary’s allusion to Nahusha, who was cast down from Indra’s throne by the curse of the sage Agastya. Modern commentators generalize: Solomon Pappaiah speaks of a ruler losing office midway, and Kalaignar reads it politically as tyranny collapsing when principled people rise up. The text is identical in both sources.

tamil:
இறந்தமைந்த சார்புடையர் ஆயினும் உய்யார்
சிறந்தமைந்த சீரார் செறின்.
transliteration:
Irandhamaindha saarputaiyar aayinum uyyaar
sirandhamaindha seeraar serin.
current_meaning: Even people with endless support and powerful friends cannot escape if truly great people become angry with them.
elementary: Having lots of friends to stick up for you is great, but if you do something really wrong to a truly good and respected person, even all those friends can’t save you. Being respectful is better protection than having a big gang.
university: The final couplet sets iRandhu amaindha saarbu (இறந்தமைந்த சார்பு, supports exceeding all measure, from iRa, to go beyond) against siRandhu amaindha seeraar (சிறந்தமைந்த சீரார், those whose glory is excellently formed). The verb uyyaar (உய்யார், they will not survive) echoes kural 896, and seRin (செறின், if angered) echoes 895 and 897, rounding off the chapter. Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary, glosses the great here as the noble whose penance is boundless, so the chapter ends where it began, with the two kinds of greatness, worldly and spiritual. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads iRandhamaindha as like the dead, that is renunciants, a markedly different interpretation of the first phrase. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
மனைவிழைவார் மாண்பயன் எய்தார் வினைவிழைவார்
வேண்டாப் பொருளும் அது.
transliteration:
Manaivizhaivaar maanpayan eydhaar vinaivizhaivaar
ventaap porulum adhu.
current_meaning: Men who care only about pleasing their wives miss the greatest reward in life. People who want to get real work done stay away from this very habit.
elementary: Imagine a team captain who stops practising because he only wants to hang out at home all day. He may be comfortable, but the team never wins. People who want to do big things keep their comfort in balance with their work.
university: The chapter title penvazhich seral (பெண்வழிச் சேறல்) literally means 'going by a woman's way', and Parimelazhagar frames the whole chapter as advice to a ruler or man of affairs within the Porul (polity) section, placed among other vices to be avoided (chapters 92-94 on wanton women, drink and gambling). In this opening couplet manai-vizhaivaar (மனைவிழைவார், those who crave the wife or household pleasure) fail to reach maan-payan (மாண்பயன், the excellent fruit), which Parimelazhagar glosses as aram (virtue), while vinai-vizhaivaar (வினைவிழைவார், those who desire action) reject such indulgence as a hindrance to porul (wealth-making). Textual note: ytamizh and thirukkural.net read the third word as vinaivizhaiyaar (வினைவிழையார், 'those who do not desire action'), while thirukkural.com, kuraltheni.com and Parimelazhagar's own gloss read vinaivizhaivaar; we follow the latter. Also note that thirukkural.com wrongly prints Kalaignar's gloss for Kural 801 under this verse. Modern critics point out that the chapter assumes a male, elite reader and a patriarchal household; many contemporary readers (including Mu. Varadarasanar's 'considering domestic comfort paramount') take its target to be infatuation and neglect of duty rather than women as such, a reading supported by Valluvar's high praise of the wife in chapter 6 (வாழ்க்கைத் துணைநலம்).

tamil:
பேணாது பெண்விழைவான் ஆக்கம் பெரியதோர்
நாணாக நாணுத் தரும்.
transliteration:
Penaadhu penvizhaivaan aakkam periyadhor
naanaaka naanuth tharum.
current_meaning: If a man forgets his duties and lives only for his desire for his wife, whatever success he has will bring him great shame that everyone can see.
elementary: If a class president stops doing the job and just lets his best friend decide everything, the whole class feels let down, and he ends up embarrassed too. Holding a job means doing it yourself.
university: Penaadhu (பேணாது, 'without guarding/caring for') is read by Parimelazhagar as neglecting one's own aanmai (ஆண்மை, manliness, i.e. capacity for independent action), while pen-vizhaivaan (பெண்விழைவான்) is one who desires the 'femininity' of his wife. The aakkam (ஆக்கம், prosperity) he holds becomes a periyadhor naan (பெரியதோர் நாண், a great shame) first for men generally and then for himself; Parimelazhagar explains that because the wife effectively controls the giving and enjoyment of that wealth, the public sees the man's agency as transferred to her. Manakkudavar reads penaadhu as neglecting aram and porul (virtue and wealth). Kalaignar's modern gloss shifts the emphasis to a man who abandons his principles to chase a woman, illustrating the trend among twentieth-century commentators to recast the chapter as a critique of infatuation rather than of women's agency. The text is uniform across ytamizh, thirukkural.net, thirukkural.com and kuraltheni. Contemporary critics note that the verse's notion of 'shame to all men' reflects a gendered honour code of its era.

tamil:
இல்லாள்கண் தாழ்ந்த இயல்பின்மை எஞ்ஞான்றும்
நல்லாருள் நாணுத் தரும்.
transliteration:
Illaalkan thaazhndha iyalpinmai egngnaandrum
nallaarul naanuth tharum.
current_meaning: A man who always gives in and bows low to his wife will feel ashamed whenever he is among good people.
elementary: If you are always too scared to say what you think, even to someone you love, you may feel awkward around friends who speak up honestly. Love works best when both people can speak freely.
university: Iyalpinmai (இயல்பின்மை) means 'that which is not natural', and Parimelazhagar glosses the whole phrase as the fear (achcham) that makes a man stoop (thaazh) before his wife; within his patriarchal frame, it is 'unnatural' because he expects the wife to be the deferential one. He adds that when a husband is so cowed, no one guides the household and every fault follows, so he is ashamed among the nallaar (நல்லார், the good) at all times (எஞ்ஞான்றும்). Manakkudavar reads it simply as the ruinous habit of stooping to the wife. Kalaignar narrows it to a husband who fails to correct a wife lacking good character, and Solomon Pappaiah stresses fear, showing modern commentators softening the verse toward a critique of timidity. The text is identical in all four sources consulted. Modern readers rightly note that the assumption that deference is natural only for wives is a historical norm, not a universal truth, while the verse's underlying point about a fear-driven partnership remains discussable.

tamil:
மனையாளை அஞ்சும் மறுமையி லாளன்
வினையாண்மை வீறெய்த லின்று.
transliteration:
Manaiyaalai anjum marumaiyi laalan
vinaiyaanmai veereydha lindru.
current_meaning: A man who is afraid of his wife loses the good that leads to a happy next life. Even if he is skilled at his work, it will never win him praise.
elementary: A painter who is too afraid of anyone's opinion to paint what he really sees will never make a great painting. Fear holds back good work.
university: Marumai-ilaalan (மறுமையிலாளன்) means 'one without (merit for) the next world'; Parimelazhagar explains that such a man cannot perform the duties of the householder (illaram) properly and so loses the reward of the hereafter. Vinai-aanmai (வினையாண்மை, the capacity to direct undertakings) may exist, but it will not attain veeru (வீறு, distinction, acclaim) among the good, because one who lacks his own nature cannot bring work to completion. Manakkudavar adds that this verse means such a man will not create wealth. Textual note: ytamizh, thirukkural.net and thirukkural.com divide the line as 'வீறெய்த லின்று' while kuraltheni prints 'வீறெய்தல் இன்று'; this is a difference of word-spacing (சீர் division vs. word division), not wording. Kalaignar gives a distinctive modern reading, taking the man as one who fears to undertake married life at all, a reinterpretation that avoids the gendered fear. Contemporary critics observe that the verse links domestic authority to public efficacy in a way typical of premodern political ethics.

tamil:
இல்லாளை அஞ்சுவான் அஞ்சுமற் றெஞ்ஞான்றும்
நல்லார்க்கு நல்ல செயல்.
transliteration:
Illaalai anjuvaan anjumat regngnaandrum
nallaarkku nalla seyal.
current_meaning: A man who is afraid of his wife will always be afraid even to do good things for good people.
elementary: If you are scared to share your snack with a hungry classmate because someone might be cross with you, fear is stopping you from being kind. Kindness needs a little courage.
university: Parimelazhagar glosses nallaar (நல்லார், the good) as gods, ascetics, the wise, one's two elders (parents) and worthy guests, and nalla seyal (நல்ல செயல்) as giving them what they need; even when the wealth is his own earning, the fearful husband hesitates. He supports the reading with a parallel from the Jain Tamil epic Civaka Cintamani (மண்மகள் 217): 'illaalai anji virunthin mugam kondra nenjin pullaalan', a man who, fearing his wife, turned away the face of a guest. Manakkudavar sums the verse as meaning such a man cannot practise aram (virtue). Kalaignar inverts the sense, reading that a man anxious not to err in doing good will heed a watchful wife, a strikingly egalitarian modern reinterpretation. The text is identical across the four sources. Critics note that the verse presumes hospitality and charity are the husband's prerogative, a presumption that modern readers can retain as a call to generosity without its gendered frame.

tamil:
இமையாரின் வாழினும் பாடிலரே இல்லாள்
அமையார்தோள் அஞ்சு பவர்.
transliteration:
Imaiyaarin vaazhinum paatilare illaal
amaiyaardhol anju pavar.
current_meaning: Even if they live as grandly as the gods, men who fear their wife's slender, bamboo-like arms have no real honour.
elementary: A superhero with amazing powers is not much of a hero if he is too scared to act. What makes someone admirable is courage, not just strength or riches.
university: Imaiyaar (இமையார், 'the unblinking ones') is a classical Tamil epithet for the gods; paatu (பாடு) here means dignity or worth, and paatilar those lacking it. Amai-aar-thol (அமையார்தோள்) compares the wife's shoulders or arms to amai (bamboo), a conventional image of feminine grace; Parimelazhagar notes that the slender image heightens the irony: a warrior who conquered heroes' arms yet fears these gentle ones has no aanmai (manliness). He reads 'living like the gods' as the life of heroes who reached heaven through valour, and says this verse closes a group of four (903-906) on the fault of fearing the wife. Manakkudavar takes it to mean that even the wealthy are not respected by others. Kalaignar again reinterprets, aiming the criticism at men who submit to a wife merely for beauty, not for wisdom or character. The text is uniform across sources. Modern critics note the verse's equation of dignity with masculine dominance as a historically situated value.

tamil:
பெண்ணேவல் செய்தொழுகும் ஆண்மையின் நாணுடைப்
பெண்ணே பெருமை உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Penneval seydhozhukum aanmaiyin naanutaip
penne perumai utaiththu.
current_meaning: A woman who has modesty and self-respect is worth far more than a man whose so-called manliness is spent doing whatever his wife orders.
elementary: Being a grown-up does not mean being bossy, and it does not mean just following orders either. A person with self-respect, whoever they are, deserves more admiration than someone who has given up thinking for themselves.
university: Pen-eval (பெண்ணேவல்) is 'a woman's command', and the man who 'conducts himself doing it' (seydhu ozhugum) is contrasted with naanutaip penne (நாணுடைப் பெண்ணே), the woman possessed of naan (நாண், modesty, sense of shame). Parimelazhagar notes that 'modest woman' is added deliberately as the opposite of the shameless man: the wife who issues commands is not the point of comparison, but rather womanhood marked by naan, which he regards as superior to such manhood. He also observes the emphatic separation of 'penne' at the line's start. Manakkudavar reads that such men are not respected by others. The verse is notable because, within its gendered frame, it affirms that a woman's perumai (பெருமை, greatness) can exceed a man's; modern feminist readers note, however, that it values women for modesty while denying men the role of following a woman. Text is identical across sources.

tamil:
நட்டார் குறைமுடியார் நன்றாற்றார் நன்னுதலாள்
பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகு பவர்.
transliteration:
Nattaar kuraimutiyaar nandraatraar nannudhalaal
pettaangu ozhuku pavar.
current_meaning: Men who live only as their lovely wife wishes will not help their friends in need, and they will not do any good deeds.
elementary: If you only ever do what one person wants, you might forget to help your other friends when they need you. Good friends keep room in their life for everyone who counts on them.
university: Nattaar (நட்டார்) are those who have formed friendship (natpu), and kurai mudiyaar (குறைமுடியார்) means they will not fulfil their friends' needs; nandru aatraar (நன்றாற்றார்) means they will not perform good deeds, which Parimelazhagar specifies as aram that aids the next world. Nan-nudhalaal (நன்னுதலாள், 'she of the fair forehead') is a conventional epithet he compares with 'bamboo-like shoulders' in 906, and pettaangu (பெட்டாங்கு) means 'as she desires'. His reasoning is that the wife cannot herself command and give wealth for these purposes, so both this-worldly and other-worldly duties lapse. Fitting the chapter's place in the Natpiyal (friendship) section, the verse highlights obligations to friends. The text is uniform across sources; Sivayogi Sivakumar's playful gloss reading pettaangu as 'like a pottu (forehead mark)' is a modern pun, not the classical sense. Modern readers may take the general point that any single relationship which crowds out duties to friends and community is unhealthy.

tamil:
அறவினையும் ஆன்ற பொருளும் பிறவினையும்
பெண்ஏவல் செய்வார்கண் இல்.
transliteration:
Aravinaiyum aandra porulum piravinaiyum
peneval seyvaarkan il.
current_meaning: Men who simply do whatever their wives command will have no good deeds, no well-earned money, and none of life's other joys either.
elementary: A good life has three parts: being kind, working hard, and having fun. If someone lets another person run every part of their life, they can end up missing all three.
university: This verse maps directly onto the three aims of the Kural itself: aram (அறம், virtue), porul (பொருள், wealth) and, as Parimelazhagar glosses pira-vinai (பிறவினை, 'other deeds'), inbam (இன்பம், pleasure). He explains that once virtue and wealth are gone, even pleasure is lost because its direction lies with the wife, and he notes that verses 907-909 together treat the fault of doing the wife's bidding (eval). Manakkudavar adds that even men without fear, if they simply obey, lose all three. Textual note: some editions print pen-eval as one word (பெண்ணேவல்), as in 907, while all four sources consulted print 'பெண்ஏவல்' here. Kalaignar narrows the target to men enslaved by arrogant women's orders, a reading that limits the claim. Contemporary scholars stress that Valluvar's ideal of the wife elsewhere (chapter 6) is a partner who safeguards the household, and that the chapter's real target is the abdication of one's own judgment.

tamil:
எண்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சத் திடனுடையார்க்கு எஞ்ஞான்றும்
பெண்சேர்ந்தாம் பேதைமை இல்.
transliteration:
Enserndha nenjath thitanutaiyaarkku egngnaandrum
penserndhaam pedhaimai il.
current_meaning: People whose minds are full of careful thought and who are strong inside will never fall into the foolishness of being ruled by love for a woman.
elementary: When you think things through and stay steady inside, you do not get swept away by any one wish or person. A calm, thoughtful mind keeps you in charge of your own choices.
university: En-serndha nenjam (எண்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சம்) is 'a mind joined to deliberation'; Parimelazhagar takes it as a mind engaged in planning affairs of state, and reads idan (இடன்) not as 'firmness' (as some modern glosses do) but as 'wealth/means', citing Kural 218 ('இடனில் பருவத்தும்') and Kalittokai to establish that sense. Ytamizh's 'thitan' transliteration reflects the sandhi 'நெஞ்சத் திடன்', which modern commentators such as Kalaignar and Mu. Varadarasanar also read as thidan (திடன், firmness of mind), so both readings circulate. Pen-serndhaam pedhaimai (பெண்சேர்ந்தாம் பேதைமை) is the folly arising from attachment to the wife; Parimelazhagar says this folly is the root of all three faults treated earlier, namely desiring, fearing and obeying, so the closing verse sums up the chapter negatively. Manakkudavar explains en-serdhal as discerning the faults that arise from such attachment. Read today, the chapter's enduring core is this closing ideal of deliberative self-command, while its gendered framing belongs to its historical setting.

tamil:
அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும் ஆய்தொடியார்
இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்.
transliteration:
Anbin vizhaiyaar porulvizhaiyum aaydhodiyaar
insol izhukkuth tharum.
current_meaning: The sweet words of bangle-wearing women who want a man's money, not his love, will in the end bring him shame and trouble.
elementary: Imagine a kid who suddenly calls you their best friend every day you bring a big bag of candy, and ignores you on days you bring nothing. Their nice words feel good, but they were never about you, and trusting them only ends with hurt feelings. Real friendship is liking someone, not liking what they can give you.
university: The opening couplet sets the chapter’s key contrast between anbu (அன்பு, love) and porul (பொருள், wealth): the women described here vizhaiyaar, ‘do not desire’, out of love but porul-vizhaiyum, ‘desire wealth’. Aaydhodiyaar (ஆய்தொடியார், ‘those wearing choice bangles’) is a conventional ornamental epithet, and the danger lies in their insol (இன்சொல், sweet speech), the same virtue Valluvar praises in chapter 10, here turned into a tool of profit. Izhukku (இழுக்கு) means both moral lapse and resulting disgrace; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah render it as ‘suffering’, Sivayogi Sivakumar as ‘degradation’. Parimelazhagar places the chapter in the Natpiyal (section on friendship) right after Penvazhicheral (being led by one’s wife), and reads it as a warning against an intimacy that only imitates friendship. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும் பண்பின் மகளிர்
நயன்தூக்கி நள்ளா விடல்.
transliteration:
Payandhookkip panburaikkum panbin magalir
nayandhookki nallaa vidal.
current_meaning: Some women of bad character first weigh what they can get from a man, then speak sweetly to him. Think about what they are really like, and stay away.
elementary: Some people check how much pocket money you have before deciding how friendly to be, and then talk about how loyal they are. Valluvar says: notice that pattern, think about it, and do not get close to someone who measures you by your wallet.
university: The couplet rests on a play of the verb thookku (தூக்கு, ‘to weigh, to measure’): the women payan-thookki, ‘weigh the profit’, so the wise man must nayan-thookki, ‘weigh their character’, and then nallaa vidal (நள்ளா விடல்), ‘leave without joining’. There is also deliberate irony in panburaikkum panbin magalir, ‘women of no virtue (panbu) who speak of virtue’: the speech is a performance tuned to the size of the purse. Puliyur Kesigan reads nayan as their behaviour, while Mu. Varadarasanar takes it as the ‘pleasure’ they offer, which the wise man evaluates and declines. Parimelazhagar treats the couplet as a practical rule of discernment rather than a moral sermon, in keeping with the Porutpal’s concern with prudent conduct. No textual variants appear between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம் இருட்டறையில்
ஏதில் பிணந்தழீஇ அற்று.
transliteration:
Porutpendir poimmai muyakkam iruttaraiyil
edhil pinandhazheei atru.
current_meaning: The fake hug of a woman who wants only money is like hugging a stranger's dead body in a dark room.
elementary: Think of hugging a big cardboard cut-out of a friend in the dark. It is shaped like a person, but nobody is really there to hug you back. Valluvar says that affection bought with money is like that: it looks like love, but there is no real heart inside it.
university: Kural 913 is the chapter’s most startling simile. Porut-pendir (பொருட்பெண்டிர், ‘women of wealth’, i.e. women who are for wealth) offer a poimmai muyakkam (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம், false embrace), compared to clasping an edhil pinam (ஏதில் பிணம், a stranger’s corpse) in an iruttarai (இருட்டறை, dark room). Parimelazhagar’s gloss, followed by Puliyur Kesigan and by the bracketed ‘(hired men)’ in the standard English explanation, explains the image: it is the hired corpse-bearer who handles an unknown body in the dark for pay, without any bond, so the transaction is equally loveless on both sides. Kalaignar reads it as acting out love purely for money. The form thazheei (தழீஇ) is an alapedai (lengthened vowel) form of thazhuvi, ‘having embraced’. Both base sources agree on the text.

tamil:
பொருட்பொருளார் புன்னலந் தோயார் அருட்பொருள்
ஆயும் அறிவி னவர்.
transliteration:
Porutporulaar punnalan thoyaar arutporul
aayum arivi navar.
current_meaning: Wise people, who look for the true treasure of kindness, will not touch the cheap charms of women whose only goal is money.
elementary: If you are saving up for something really valuable, like a bicycle, you do not spend it all on sweets that are gone in a minute. Wise people treat their hearts the same way: they look for real kindness, not for ‘friendships’ that are only about money.
university: The couplet turns on a pun on porul: porut-porulaar (பொருட்பொருளார்) are ‘those whose object (porul) is wealth (porul)’, set against arut-porul (அருட்பொருள்), ‘the wealth that is arul (grace, compassion)’, which the wise aayum (ஆயும், examine and pursue). Punnalam (புன்னலம், ‘petty or base beauty’) is the low pleasure they decline, and thoyaar (தோயார்) means ‘will not immerse themselves in or touch’. Mu. Varadarasanar treats arul itself as the highest wealth, while Solomon Pappaiah reads arut-porul as ‘wealth sought together with compassion’, a reading in keeping with Parimelazhagar’s concern that riches be earned and used with arul. The echo of chapter 25 (Aruludaimai) is deliberate. Ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree, with punnalan(th) sandhi spelled புன்னலந்.

tamil:
பொதுநலத்தார் புன்னலம் தோயார் மதிநலத்தின்
மாண்ட அறிவி னவர்.
transliteration:
Podhunalaththaar punnalam thoyaar madhinalaththin
maanda arivi navar.
current_meaning: People whose wisdom has been made strong by good sense will not go after the cheap pleasures of women who give themselves to anyone who pays.
elementary: A smart kid who knows what real friendship is will not chase someone who is ‘best friends’ with whoever gives the most presents that day. Good sense helps you see that kind of friendship is not really for you at all.
university: Podhu-nalaththaar (பொதுநலத்தார்) means ‘those whose charms (nalam) are common (podhu)’, available to all who pay. Valluvar sets this against mathi-nalam (மதிநலம்), ‘the excellence of natural intelligence’, which makes knowledge maandu (மாண்ட, perfected, excellent). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan distinguish iyarkai arivu (inborn sense) from acquired learning, and Kalaignar explicitly names both ‘natural intelligence and learned knowledge’, following Parimelazhagar’s distinction between mathi (native wit) and arivu (learning). The couplet is built parallel to 914 (punnalam thoyaar repeats), so the pair should be read together: 914 names the motive of the wise (arul), 915 the faculty (mathi). Both base sources give the same text.

tamil:
தந்நலம் பாரிப்பார் தோயார் தகைசெருக்கிப்
புன்னலம் பாரிப்பார் தோள்.
transliteration:
Thannalam paarippaar thoyaar thagaiserukkip
punnalam paarippaar thol.
current_meaning: People who care about their own good name will not go to the arms of women who show off their charm and sell cheap pleasures to anyone.
elementary: If you care about being known as honest and kind, you will be careful about who you spend your time with. You would not team up with someone who sells their ‘friendship’ to anyone, because you value your good name.
university: The couplet repeats the verb paarippaar (பாரிப்பார்) in two senses: those who paarippaar thannalam, ‘cherish or spread their own goodness (or fame)’, will not touch the shoulders of those who paarippaar punnalam, ‘spread their petty charms abroad’. Thagai-serukki (தகைசெருக்கி) is ‘being proud of their attractiveness or skill’. Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesigan take thannalam as one’s own fame, Mu. Varadarasanar as one’s ‘good conduct’, and Parimelazhagar as the reputation that comes from virtue. Textual note: thirukkural.net prints the first verb as பாரப்பார் (paarappaar), whereas ytamizh.com and the standard Parimelazhagar text read பாரிப்பார்; the repeated verb and all four commentaries support பாரிப்பார், so the variant looks like a typographical slip.

tamil:
நிறைநெஞ்சம் இல்லவர் தோய்வார் பிறநெஞ்சிற்
பேணிப் புணர்பவர் தோள்.
transliteration:
Nirainenjam illavar thoyvaar piranenjir
penip punarpavar thol.
current_meaning: Only people without a steady, self-controlled heart will go to the arms of women who hug them while their own hearts are set on someone else.
elementary: Someone who is pretending to be your friend while really thinking about your video games is not giving you their heart. Valluvar says only a person who cannot control their own wishes keeps running after friends like that.
university: Nirai-nenjam (நிறைநெஞ்சம்) is ‘a full or restrained heart’; nirai is the classical virtue of self-control, the power to hold the mind in check, which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses as ‘the strength to rule one’s heart’. The women are those who embrace while pira-nenjil peni (பிறநெஞ்சிற் பேணி), ‘cherishing something else in their heart’, which Puliyur Kesigan and Solomon Pappaiah identify as the money they want. The couplet thus contrasts two divided states: the women’s hearts are elsewhere, and the men lack a governed heart of their own. Parimelazhagar connects nirai with the self-mastery praised in chapter 13 (Adakkamudaimai). Both base sources agree on the text.

tamil:
ஆயும் அறிவினர் அல்லார்க்கு அணங்கென்ப
மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு.
transliteration:
Aayum arivinar allaarkku anangenba
maaya magalir muyakku.
current_meaning: For people without the sense to look closely, the hug of tricky, false women is said to be like being grabbed by a demon that leads them to harm.
elementary: In fairy tales, a magic song can make people forget who they are and walk into trouble. Valluvar says that people who do not stop to think can be ‘enchanted’ by false affection in the same way, while thoughtful people can see the trick.
university: Anangu (அணங்கு) in Sangam usage is a dangerous divine power, often a female spirit that seizes and afflicts; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as anangu-thaakku, ‘the attack of an anangu’, and as ‘Mohini’s bewitchment’, and Solomon Pappaiah as ‘a deity who stirs desire and takes life’. Maaya magalir (மாய மகளிர்) are women skilled in maayam (மாயம், deception, illusion). The decisive phrase is aayum arivinar allaar (ஆயும் அறிவினர் அல்லார்), ‘those who are not of examining intelligence’: only they experience this as a supernatural seizure, whereas the discerning see an ordinary deception. Enba (என்ப, ‘they say’) marks this as received opinion. Sivayogi Sivakumar alone reads anangu in the positive sense of ‘divine’, as what the foolish mistake such embraces for. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
வரைவிலா மாணிழையார் மென்தோள் புரையிலாப்
பூரியர்கள் ஆழும் அளறு.
transliteration:
Varaivilaa maanizhaiyaar mendhol puraiyilaap
pooriyargal aazhum alaru.
current_meaning: The soft arms of jewel-wearing women who keep no limits are like a deep, hellish swamp that low and foolish men sink into.
elementary: Picture a pretty field that is really a deep mud bog. It looks soft and inviting, but anyone who walks in without thinking gets stuck and sinks. Valluvar says that ‘love’ that is only bought and sold is like that bog.
university: This couplet supplies the chapter’s title word: varaivilaa (வரைவிலா), ‘without varaivu’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses varaivu as ‘a moral limit’ (ozhukka varaiyarai), and Puliyur Kesigan and Solomon Pappaiah as ‘not distinguishing between high and low’ among those who pay; in akam poetry varaivu also means ‘marriage’, which yields the reading ‘women outside wedlock’. Maanizhaiyaar (மாணிழையார்) is ‘those with fine jewels’. Alaru (அளறு) means both mire or mud and naraka (hell), and the commentators exploit both: Kalaignar speaks of ‘the mire called hell’. Puraiyilaa pooriyargal (புரையிலாப் பூரியர்கள்) are ‘base men without worth’; Sivayogi Sivakumar takes purai as ‘fault’, so ‘those who do not know what is wrong’. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
இருமனப் பெண்டிரும் கள்ளும் கவறும்
திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Irumanap pendirum kallum kavarum
thiruneekkap pattaar thodarbu.
current_meaning: Two-faced women, alcohol and gambling are the friends of people whom good luck has left behind.
elementary: Imagine a kid who spends all their allowance on silly gambling games at the fair, sugary junk, and ‘friends’ who only like them for their money. Soon the money is gone and so are the ‘friends’. Valluvar says these habits are a sign that someone’s good luck is slipping away.
university: The closing couplet groups three ruinous attachments: irumanap pendir (இருமனப் பெண்டிர், ‘women of two minds’, whose heart is in one place and body in another, as Solomon Pappaiah explains), kal (கள், toddy or liquor) and kavaru (கவறு, dice).
