Their thodarbu (தொடர்பு, ‘association’) belongs to those thiru-neekkap-pattaar (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார்), ‘those from whom Thiru has been removed’; Thiru is both fortune and the goddess Lakshmi (Thirumagal), which is how Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan read it. Parimelazhagar notes that the couplet links this chapter to the next two, Kallunnaamai (93, not drinking) and Soodhu (94, gambling), so it works as a hinge for the whole cluster of vices. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
உட்கப் படாஅர் ஒளியிழப்பர் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
கட்காதல் கொண்டொழுகு வார்.
transliteration:
Utkap pataaar oliyizhappar enjnjaandrum
katkaadhal kondozhugu vaar.
current_meaning: People who always crave alcohol will never be feared by their enemies, and they will lose the good name they once had.
elementary: Imagine a strong, respected team captain who starts doing something silly every day. Soon nobody on the other team worries about him any more, and even his own friends stop looking up to him. The Kural says a love of strong drink does exactly that: it makes a person look small.
university: The chapter opens with two losses: the drinker is not utkappadaar (உட்கப்படாஅர், 'not feared', from உட்கு, awe or dread, with an alapedai lengthening) and he oliyizhappar (ஒளியிழப்பர், 'loses his lustre'), where oli (ஒளி) means both brightness and reputation. The habitual sense comes from katkaadhal kondozhuguvaar (கட்காதல் கொண்டொழுகுவார்), 'those who conduct themselves holding a love of toddy', so the target is addiction rather than a single lapse. Because the chapter sits in Porutpaal beside Varaivin Magalir (92) and Soothu (94), the traditional reading inherited from Parimelazhagar treats it as one of the vices a ruler must shun; Puliyur Kesikan's gloss on thirukkural.net explicitly makes the subject 'kings' whose enemies no longer fear them and who lose the fame won by their ancestors. Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the subject general. The couplet is identical on ytamizh and thirukkural.net, though the two sites attach the Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar glosses in opposite order.

tamil:
உண்ணற்க கள்ளை உணில்உண்க சான்றோரான்
எண்ணப் படவேண்டா தார்.
transliteration:
Unnarka kallai unilunka saandroraan
ennap padavendaa thaar.
current_meaning: Do not drink alcohol. If anyone wants to drink, let it be only those who do not care whether good and wise people respect them.
elementary: Suppose a teacher says, ‘Don't cheat on the test. Well, if you really want to cheat, go ahead, but only if you don't care whether anyone ever trusts you again.’ The teacher isn't giving permission. She is showing how much it costs. The Kural speaks about drinking the same way.
university: The first clause is a flat prohibition, unnarka kallai (உண்ணற்க கள்ளை, 'drink not toddy'). The second, unil unka (உணில் உண்க, 'if you would drink, drink'), is an ironic concession, a figure the commentators call igazhchchi (இகழ்ச்சி, scorn). It limits the 'permission' to those who are saandroraan ennappada vendaathaar (சான்றோரான் எண்ணப்பட வேண்டாதார்), people who do not wish to be esteemed by the saandror (சான்றோர், the noble and learned). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all keep this ironic reading. Puliyur Kesikan adds that the first clause is addressed to arivudaiyor (the wise), since toddy clouds the mind. The structure foreshadows Kural 923, where the saandror again sit in judgment. The text is identical on both base sites.

tamil:
ஈன்றாள் முகத்தேயும் இன்னாதால் என்மற்றுச்
சான்றோர் முகத்துக் களி.
transliteration:
Eendraal mugaththeyum innaadhaal enmatruch
chaandror mugaththuk kali.
current_meaning: Being drunk is painful to see even for the mother who gave birth to you. How much worse must it look to the wise?
elementary: Your mom loves you no matter what, even after you spill juice on the carpet. But some behaviour makes even a loving mom sad and embarrassed. If something upsets the person who forgives you most, imagine how it looks to a strict teacher or a respected elder.
university: The couplet argues from the lesser to the greater. Eendraal (ஈன்றாள், 'she who bore') is the most forgiving witness a person has; Puliyur Kesikan glosses her as the one who rejoices whatever her child does. Even 'in her face' (mugaththeyum, முகத்தேயும்) kali (களி, intoxication) is innaadhu (இன்னாது, painful). The question en matru (என் மற்று, 'what, then?') carries the argument to the saandror (சான்றோர்), whom Mu. Varadarasanar describes as having the nature of rebuking faults (குற்றம் கடியும் இயல்பு). The repeated mugam (முகம், face) presents shame as something seen. Kalaignar reads the subject as the son his mother cannot bear to look at. The text is identical on both base sites.

tamil:
நாண்என்னும் நல்லாள் புறங்கொடுக்கும் கள்ளென்னும்
பேணாப் பெருங்குற்றத் தார்க்கு.
transliteration:
Naanennum nallaal purangodukkum kallennum
penaap perungutrath thaarkku.
current_meaning: The good lady called Shame (the feeling that stops us from doing wrong) turns her back on those who commit the great, hateful wrong of drinking.
elementary: Picture Modesty as a kind lady who walks beside you and whispers ‘don't do that, it's embarrassing.’ The Kural says that when someone gets drunk she turns around and walks away, so there's no one left to stop him doing shameful things.
university: Naan (நாண், modesty, the sense of shame) is personified as a nallaal (நல்லாள், a good woman). Purangodukkum (புறங்கொடுக்கும்), literally 'gives the back', is a battlefield term for retreat, so Modesty flees from the drinker as a beaten warrior flees. The parallel compounds naanennum nallaal / kallennum penaap perungutram (கள்ளென்னும் பேணாப் பெருங்குற்றம், 'the great fault called toddy, which none would cherish') set a personified virtue against a personified vice. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses that she will not stand before the drinker; Solomon Pappaiah renders it as Modesty showing her back and going away. The idea looks ahead to Naanudaimai (chapter 102). The text is identical on both base sites.

tamil:
கையறி யாமை உடைத்தே பொருள்கொடுத்து
மெய்யறி யாமை கொளல்.
transliteration:
Kaiyari yaamai udaiththe porulkoduththu
meyyari yaamai kolal.
current_meaning: Paying money just to buy a state where you no longer know yourself shows that you do not understand what you are doing.
elementary: Imagine spending all your pocket money on a ticket for a ride that makes you so dizzy you can't remember your own name, and then trips you over. You'd be paying to lose yourself. The Kural says buying liquor is that kind of bad deal.
university: The couplet balances two forms of ignorance: kaiyariyaamai (கையறியாமை) and meyyariyaamai (மெய்யறியாமை). The second clearly means not knowing one's own body or self, the stupor that porul koduththu (பொருள்கொடுத்து, 'by giving wealth') one kolal (கொளல், 'takes on'). The first is read in two ways. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as not knowing what to do, a failure of practical sense. Puliyur Kesikan (thirukkural.net) reads it as having one's past karma as its cause, so only an ill-fated person would make such a bargain. Kalaignar calls it folly beyond words. The Kural's irony is economic: wealth, the subject of Porutpaal, is spent to buy unawareness. The text is identical on both base sites.

tamil:
துஞ்சினார் செத்தாரின் வேறல்லர் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
நஞ்சுண்பார் கள்ளுண் பவர்.
transliteration:
Thunjinaar seththaarin verallar enjnjaandrum
nanjunpaar kallun pavar.
current_meaning: People who are asleep are no different from the dead. In the same way, people who drink alcohol are always no different from people who drink poison.
elementary: When someone is fast asleep, they can't see, hear or help anyone, almost as if they weren't there at all. The Kural says drinking liquor is like taking a little poison: it switches off your mind the same way.
university: The couplet is an udhaaranam (உதாரணம், exemplum) built on two equations. Thunjinaar (துஞ்சினார், those asleep) are 'not different from' (verallar, வேறல்லர்) seththaar (செத்தார், the dead), because both lack awareness. Likewise kallunbavar (கள்ளுண்பவர், toddy-drinkers) are always nanjunbaar (நஞ்சுண்பார், poison-eaters). Mu. Varadarasanar gives the shared term as arivu mayangudhal (அறிவு மயங்குதல், clouding of understanding). Puliyur Kesikan applies enjnjaandrum (எஞ்ஞான்றும், 'always') to the second clause: the drinker is permanently poisoned, while the sleeper only appears dead for a while. Kalaignar reverses the order and reads it as a hyperbole. The text is identical on both base sites.

tamil:
உள்ளொற்றி உள்ளூர் நகப்படுவர் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
கள்ளொற்றிக் கண்சாய் பவர்.
transliteration:
Ullotri ulloor nagappaduvar enjnjaandrum
kallotrik kansaai pavar.
current_meaning: People who drink in secret until their eyes droop will have their secret found out by the people of their town, who will always laugh at them.
elementary: If you sneak cookies before dinner, the crumbs on your shirt give you away. The Kural says people who drink in secret are the same: their sleepy, drooping eyes tell everyone, and the whole neighbourhood ends up laughing.
university: The verb otri (ஒற்றி, 'in hiding') is used twice. Kal otri (கள்ளொற்றி) is drinking toddy secretly, and ul otri (உள்ளொற்றி) is the townsfolk spying out what is inside. Kansaaibavar (கண்சாய்பவர்) are 'those whose eyes droop', the physical sign that betrays them. Ulloor (உள்ளூர், one's own town) makes the mockery (nagappaduvar, நகப்படுவர், 'will be laughed at') come from neighbours, not strangers. Mu. Varadarasanar reads ul otri as the townsfolk probing into hidden matters. Kalaignar stresses that the reeling eyes cannot be hidden. thirukkural.net prints the couplet without the closing full stop; the wording is otherwise identical on both base sites.

tamil:
களித்தறியேன் என்பது கைவிடுக நெஞ்சத்து
ஒளித்ததூஉம் ஆங்கே மிகும்.
transliteration:
Kaliththariyen enbadhu kaividuka nenjaththu
oliththadhooum aange migum.
current_meaning: A drinker should stop saying, 'I have never been drunk.' When they drink, whatever they hid in their heart comes out even more.
elementary: It's like a shaken bottle of fizzy drink: open it and everything inside comes spraying out. The Kural says drink opens people up the same way, so pretending you never drink doesn't work. Your secrets fizz out the moment you do.
university: Kaliththariyen (களித்தறியேன்) is the drinker's own denial: 'I have never known intoxication.' Kaividuka (கைவிடுக, 'give it up') tells him to drop the lie. The reason is nenjaththu oliththadhooum (நெஞ்சத்து ஒளித்ததூஉம், 'even what was hidden in the heart'; the -ooum is an alapedai of -um, 'even') aange migum (ஆங்கே மிகும், 'there and then increases', that is, comes out all the more). Mu. Varadarasanar reads the hidden thing as the hidden fault; Puliyur Kesikan as the earlier concealment of drinking itself; Kalaignar as the truth that the drunk man blurts out. The idea is close to the Graeco-Roman proverb 'in wine, truth'. The text is identical on both base sites.

tamil:
களித்தானைக் காரணம் காட்டுதல் கீழ்நீர்க்
குளித்தானைத் தீத்துரீஇ அற்று.
transliteration:
Kaliththaanaik kaaranam kaattudhal keezhneerk
kuliththaanaith theeththureei atru.
current_meaning: Trying to reason with a drunk person is like taking a burning torch under deep water to look for someone who has sunk.
elementary: Imagine your friend has dived to the bottom of a pool and you try to find him by shining a candle from the side. The water puts the flame out and you can't reach him. The Kural says giving good reasons to someone who is drunk is like that: your words can't get through.
university: Kaaranam kaattudhal (காரணம் காட்டுதல், 'showing reasons') is set against keezhneer kuliththaan (கீழ்நீர்க் குளித்தான், 'one who has plunged into deep water'), and the attempt is theeththureei atru (தீத்துரீஇ அற்று, 'like searching with fire'). Thuru (துருவுதல்) means to probe or search, and the -eei is an alapedai lengthening. The image works twice over: fire cannot burn under water, and a drowned man is beyond help. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it as trying to sober or reform the drinker with arguments. Puliyur Kesikan takes kaaranam kaattudhal as pointing to another drunk as a warning, which leads into Kural 930. The text is identical on both base sites.

tamil:
கள்ளுண்ணாப் போழ்திற் களித்தானைக் காணுங்கால்
உள்ளான்கொல் உண்டதன் சோர்வு.
transliteration:
Kallunnaap pozhdhir kaliththaanaik kaanungaal
ullaankol undadhan sorvu.
current_meaning: When a drinker is sober and sees someone else who is drunk, does he not think that he looks just as bad when he drinks?
elementary: Have you ever laughed at someone acting silly, then realised you act just like that sometimes? The Kural asks why a drinker, seeing another person drunk and stumbling, doesn't think, ‘Oh no, that's me when I drink!’
university: The closing couplet is a rhetorical question marked by kol (கொல்). When the drinker, in kallunnaap pozhdhu (கள்ளுண்ணாப் போழ்து, 'the time he is not drinking'), sees a kaliththaan (களித்தான், a drunk man), will he not reflect, ullaan (உள்ளான், 'will he not consider'), on the sorvu (சோர்வு, slackness, lapse) that comes from his own drinking? The appeal is to self-recognition. Commentators agree on this reading: Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesikan all take it as a sober drinker seeing his own condition in another. Mu. Varadarasanar's printed gloss reads மயங்கினவளை ('the intoxicated woman') on both base sites, apparently a typographical slip for மயங்கினவனை. The text is identical on ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வேண்டற்க வென்றிடினும் சூதினை வென்றதூஉம்
தூண்டிற்பொன் மீன்விழுங்கி அற்று.
transliteration:
Vendarka vendridinum soodhinai vendradhooum
thoondirpon meenvizhungi atru.
current_meaning: Do not go after gambling, even if you can win. Winning at gambling is like a fish swallowing bait with an iron hook hidden in it.
elementary: A fish sees a tasty worm and gulps it, happy for one second, but the worm hides a sharp hook. Valluvar says winning at gambling is that worm: it feels like a prize, but it pulls you in and you cannot get away.
university: The chapter opens by closing the most tempting loophole: vendridinum (வென்றிடினும், 'even should you win') concedes the gambler's best case and still forbids the desire (vendarka, வேண்டற்க). The simile turns on thoondirpon (தூண்டிற்பொன்), where pon (பொன்), usually 'gold', is read by the commentators as 'metal, iron': Mu. Varadarasanar on both ytamizh and thirukkural.net glosses it as தூண்டில் இரும்பு, 'the iron of the hook', and Kalaignar speaks of the iron barb (இரும்பு முள்). The alapedai in vendradhooum (வென்றதூஉம்) gives emphasis: even the thing won. The tradition descending from Parimelazhagar reads this chapter, like the two before it (Varaivin Magalir and Kallunnaamai), as a list of pleasures a ruler and a householder must shun, and the opening couplet sets the theme that gambling's gains are themselves the trap. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.
